# Drifted Marketing

> Drifted — a growth agency for ads, content and AI apps, founded 2026, Karachi, working New York hours. We run Meta and Google ads, make the content that feeds them and build custom AI apps, for a published monthly fee, with one number and one date written into every contract.

## Drifted Marketing in one paragraph

Drifted Marketing (also called Drifted) is a growth agency founded in 2026 by Umer Tariq, with its studio at 111-C, Murtaza Commercial, DHA Phase 8, Karachi, Pakistan. The team works New York business hours from Karachi, for brands in the United States, the Netherlands, Australia and Pakistan. It runs Meta and Google ads, makes the short-form video and social content that feeds them, does search work for Google, Google Maps and AI assistants, and builds websites, Shopify stores and custom AI apps. Its monthly fees are published, advertising spend stays in the client's own account, and every contract names one number and one date. It is not Drift, the chat software company, and not drifted.com, the motorsport publisher.

## Services

- [Performance media](https://driftedmarketing.com/services/#performance-media): Paid advertising on Meta (Instagram and Facebook) and Google, where the creative, the campaign structure and the budget are run by one team and judged against one agreed number — revenue, orders or cost per customer — by one agreed date.
- [Creator growth](https://driftedmarketing.com/services/#creator-growth): Short-form video, carousels and posts made for the stranger scrolling past rather than the follower who already knows the brand — and, for creators, turning an audience into a business with products priced to margin before anything is designed.
- [AI product](https://driftedmarketing.com/services/#ai-product): Custom AI apps built for one business's real workload — for example writing auction listings from photographs — scoped against how the tool saves time or makes money before any code is written, and checked by a person where judgement matters.
- [All services](https://driftedmarketing.com/services/): sold together, one team, one monthly fee.

## Pricing

Drifted publishes its price: $2,000 a month for one discipline, $4,000 a month for the full content and findability loop, or a tailored fee for paid media at scale and AI builds. Advertising spend is separate, stays in your own account, and we never take a percentage of it. Full page: https://driftedmarketing.com/pricing/

### Starter — $2,000 a month

One channel, one number, a brand testing whether any of this works.

Includes:
- Ads: Meta ads on one account, four new ad creatives a month, optimised weekly
- Or content: four short videos and three carousels a month
- Or search: four page optimisations, one researched article and Google Business Profile posts a month
- One of the three, picked on the first call — not all three
- A monthly written report and a monthly call

Excludes:
- Advertising spend, which is yours and stays in your account

### Standard — $4,000 a month

A brand that wants the whole loop running — content, findability and counsel.

Includes:
- Eight short videos and six carousels a month
- Four static posters a month
- Eight page optimisations a month
- Two researched articles a month, eight hundred to twelve hundred words each
- Answer-engine entries, so the brand is quotable to an assistant
- Google Business Profile maintained, with four posts a month
- Two email campaigns a month
- A visibility report, a written monthly report and a monthly call
- Four consultation hours a month

Excludes:
- Paid advertising management and advertising spend
- On-site photography and videography
- Website development

### Tailored — priced to the number

Paid media at scale, a product build, a shoot — or all three at once.

Includes:
- Paid media management across Meta and Google
- Custom AI product, scoped against how it earns before it is built
- Photography, video and production
- Everything in Standard

Excludes:
- Advertising spend, which is yours and stays in your account

We are the wrong choice if:
- You want the cheapest possible price. There is always someone cheaper, and at some point that person is a person with a template.
- You want a team of ten names on a slide. There is a small team here and the person who pitches the work does the work.
- You want us to promise a number before we have seen the account. We will give you a number on the first call, out loud — but not before we have looked.
- You need the whole thing done by Friday. Work starts in week one, the first creative is live in week three, and numbers land around week four.
- You want to own none of it. The advertising account, the pages and the creative stay yours, and that means you have to hold the keys.

## Work — every figure named to its client

Current clients: The Gallery (Pakistan) — a personalised newborn brand; Meta ads, content and the store; Frank Zoller Authentic History (United States) — a militaria auction operation; the AI listing platform, the website and its marketing; Gettysburg Museum of History (Gettysburg, Pennsylvania) — social content, short-form video, event campaigns and search visibility; ehsaan (Pakistan) — a person-to-person thrift marketplace; the app, the brand and the launch; Oorlogsspullen (Netherlands) — a militaria shop; an AI writer that drafts its product listings. Every number below is one we can produce the account for; where a result is not measured yet, no figure is given.

### Frank Zoller Authentic History — https://driftedmarketing.com/work/zoller/

Current client. Frank Zoller Authentic History, a militaria auction operation.
Case study: an AI app that writes auction listings from photographs for Frank Zoller Authentic History — 1,250 lots per auction, 400+ hours off the desk.

- 400+ hours saved.
- 1,250 lots per auction, previously typed by hand, now filled from photographs.
- Trained on a reference corpus of 32,000 items.
- Three builds for this client and counting: the listing platform, an internal inventory tool and the zollerhistory.com rebuild.

Every auction meant 1,250 lots entered by hand. Photograph, edit, renumber, then type a title, a description, a start price and an estimate range — one lot at a time, to lot 1,250.
The work was not hard. It was long, and it happened before anything could be sold, on every single auction.
- Ingestion: 32,000 past items — titles, descriptions, estimates and realized prices — ingested into a hosted backend as the model’s reference set.
- The engine: Photographs in, complete listing rows out. Repeat items pull their own history; new items get identified and described from the image.
- Review triage: Confidence-scored output. Only uncertain items are flagged for a human; everything else passes straight through.
- The handoff: The filled template uploads straight to LiveAuctioneers, and existing automation cross-posts to BidSpirit and the direct bidding site.

What we found: With 32,000 past records in one place, every estimate could be checked against what the lot actually sold for — something no one could do by hand.

### Noted. — https://driftedmarketing.com/work/noted/

Past work. A creator's merch brand; the engagement ended in September 2026.
Past work: a merch brand built for a creator with 115K followers — brand identity on a red-pen concept, an eight-product line priced to margin, a launch.

- 115K followers at launch.
- 3K new followers a month while Drifted ran it.
- 8 products, priced to margin.

115K people, consistent attention, and no product. Brand deals paid inconsistently and every merch idea died at the question nobody had answered: what does it cost to make, what does it sell for, and what is left.
- The concept: A full identity built on a red-pen annotation idea — a brand, not a logo on a shirt.
- Margin first: An eight-product line priced against real production costs, with the margin table built before anything was designed.
- Production: Printful and Tapstitch hybrid, so quality and turnaround both hold at volume.
- The launch: Instagram launch strategy, content calendar, and a handoff package so the cycle runs without us.

What we found: The audience was already there. Nothing had ever been sold to it — the constraint was structural, not creative.

### Ehsaan — https://driftedmarketing.com/work/ehsaan/

Client work. A person-to-person thrift marketplace app for Pakistan; in production.
Case study: a person-to-person thrift marketplace app for Pakistan — the app, the brand system and the launch campaign, with a first build in 23 prompts.

- 23 prompts to first build.
- A 19-section knowledge base behind the build.

Second-hand clothing in Pakistan moved through comment sections, WhatsApp groups and DM negotiations. No listings, no search, no trust layer, nothing built for the people actually using it.
- Twenty-three prompts to first build: React, Vite, TypeScript and Supabase through Lovable, then moved to Claude Code against a nineteen-section knowledge base so the product keeps its own rules as it grows.
- A Gen-Z-native brand: Identity, type system and product design built for the audience that already trades this way — fast, visual, unembarrassed about second-hand.
- The launch system: Social content, video and launch assets produced alongside the build, so the product and the campaign ship as one thing.

What we found: Trust is the product. Every design decision routed back to whether a stranger would send money for a stranger’s jacket.

### The Gallery — https://driftedmarketing.com/work/gallery/

Current client. Personalised newborn brand, Pakistan (@thegallery.bytg).
Meta ads case study: Instagram DM-first campaigns for a personalised newborn brand. $5.20–$6 back per $1 of ad spend, every campaign to July 2026.

- $5.20–$6 back per $1 of ad spend, every campaign to July 2026.
- Ten creatives in the campaign; the sale closes in Instagram DMs.

Personalised newborn gifts sell through conversation — sizing, spelling, dates, photos. The checkout was already the DM, so a campaign built to push traffic at a product page would have been measuring the wrong thing.
- Ten creatives, one job: A tight creative set built to start a conversation rather than close a cart.
- DM-native buying: Campaigns optimised toward the inbox, with the sale tracked where it actually happens.
- Weekly iteration: The losers get cut, the winners get rebuilt. The number is reported every week against what was agreed.

### Gettysburg Museum of History — https://driftedmarketing.com/work/gettysburg/

Current client since August 2026. A museum of military history in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania; short films, event campaigns and search. No figures published yet.
Case study: short films from the collection, an October anniversary campaign and search work for the Gettysburg Museum of History in Pennsylvania.

The museum keeps its collection on open display: uniforms, equipment and the stories of the men who carried them. The job was to put that collection in front of people who had not walked through the door yet, and to fill the room for the museum's October anniversary weekend.
- Short films from the collection: Every object in the cases is a story. We film the piece, write one line and cut it for vertical: who wore it, where, and why it sits behind this glass.
- The October campaign: A thirty-day run for the Band of Brothers anniversary weekend: countdown stories, an object series, an invitation film and the paid plan, all in one look.
- Search: The event page, the museum's listing and the Foundation's new site, written so the people searching for the weekend land on the museum's own page.

What we found: Objects beat adjectives. A jacket with a name on it stops the scroll.

### Legacy Blinds — https://driftedmarketing.com/work/blinds/

Client work. Paid social creative for a window-treatments brand.
Case study: a six-frame comparison carousel for a window-treatments brand, opening on the price question buyers actually ask. Built for paid social.

- A six-frame comparison carousel; reach and sales not yet published.

Linen roller shades and faux wood blinds photograph similarly and sell to the same room, so a scrolling buyer reads them as interchangeable and sorts on price alone. An ad that simply shows the product loses that comparison before it starts.
- Ask, don’t tell: The carousel opens on a question — which of these costs more — so the first frame buys a swipe instead of asking for a click.
- One product per frame: A, then A in detail, then B. Each frame carries a single claim about make and material, so the comparison is legible at thumb speed.
- Land on craft, not price: The payoff frame reframes the question it opened with: style is one thing, craftsmanship is another. The buyer arrives at the link having already argued themselves out of sorting on price.

What we found: Answering the price question directly is what earns the swipe. A carousel that opens on a claim gets scrolled past; one that opens on a question gets finished.

### Seyr — https://driftedmarketing.com/work/seyr/

Client work. Ecommerce storefront design and build.
Case study: an ecommerce storefront designed and built for Seyr — product pages, checkout path and brand, made to convert rather than to win awards.

- Conversion-built: Structure, product presentation and checkout flow designed around the purchase, not the portfolio shot.
- Handover: Client-run from day one, with the build documented.

### Multi-brand social — https://driftedmarketing.com/work/social/

Client work. Strategy, production and client communication across four brand accounts; two run directly, two early freelance work.
Strategy, production and client communication across four brand accounts. The Poster Project reached 2.2M views in 90 days, 80% of it organic.

- The Poster Project: 2.2M views in 90 days, 80% organic, from an account with 811 followers at the time.
- The Poster Project: 199,392 accounts reached, up 174.5%.
- The Poster Project: 80K accounts reached in 30 days.
- BamBam NYC, early freelance work: $0.25 per landing page view.

Four brands, small follower counts, and a category where reach is normally bought. The work was to make content that travels on its own and only pay where paying is efficient.
- One operator, four accounts: Strategy, production and client communication in one pair of hands — no coordination layer. Two of the four ran under Drifted; two are early freelance work, from before Drifted had a name.
- Organic first, paid where it pays: 80% of the Poster Project’s 2.2M views were organic. BamBam’s paid traffic, early freelance work, ran at $0.25 per landing page view.

What we found: Reach beats followers. The Poster Project reached 199,392 accounts in 90 days — up 174.5% — from what was then an 811-follower base.

## How an engagement works

1. A thirty-minute call, no deck. You bring the number you need to hit and the date; you get a yes or a no on the call.
2. The whole plan on one page, with the target written into the contract.
3. Work starts in week one; the first creative is live in week three. Numbers by week four, reported against the agreed number.
4. A written report and a call every month. Thirty days' notice to leave; the accounts, pages and creative are yours throughout.
The whole method, week by week, with the rules that do not change: https://driftedmarketing.com/process/

## Housefly — the operating system Drifted built to run the studio

Housefly is the multi-agent AI system Umer Tariq built, on his own, to run Drifted Marketing. Most of the team works beside an AI agent of their own that keeps its own memory and learns how that person works; the agents pass notes and offer tasks through a shared hive, where a note is never an order; and scheduled jobs run overnight on the studio's own machine so the work is waiting in the morning. It writes and tests the studio's own software. It multiplies the team rather than replacing it: every action that would write to a client's live account is proposed, armed with a single-use code and approved by a person, a rejection is remembered, and credentials stay out of the agent's reach. It is being prepared for a public release; there is no date. https://driftedmarketing.com/housefly/

## Questions buyers ask

### What is Drifted Marketing?

Drifted Marketing is a growth agency for ads, content and AI apps, founded in Karachi in 2026 and working New York hours for brands in the United States, the Netherlands, Australia and Pakistan. One studio plans, shoots, edits and runs the media under a published monthly fee, with one number and one date written into the contract.

### What does a growth agency in Karachi do?

Drifted is a growth agency for ads, content and AI apps, founded 2026 in Karachi and working New York hours. We run Meta and Google ads, make the content that feeds them, and build custom AI apps — one team and one monthly fee, with one number and one date written into the contract.

### How much does a performance marketing agency cost?

Drifted publishes its price: $2,000 a month for one discipline, $4,000 a month for the full content and findability loop, or a tailored fee for paid media at scale and AI builds. Advertising spend is separate, stays in your own account, and we never take a percentage of it.

### Who runs Drifted?

Umer Tariq, the founder, sets the plan and signs off every number. Drifted is a growth agency for ads, content and AI apps, founded 2026 in Karachi and working New York hours. Aahan runs the creative team and Zayan runs operations, so the people who plan your work sit with the people who shoot, cut and ship it.

### How does an engagement with a growth agency work?

Drifted, a growth agency in Karachi working New York hours, runs every engagement the same way. A thirty-minute call sets the number and the date. The plan goes on one page and into the contract. Work is live in week three, and numbers are reported against the target by week four.

### Can a Karachi agency run marketing for a US brand?

Yes. Drifted is a growth agency in Karachi that works the New York business day, so a US brand messages during its day and hears back during its day. Fees are published in US dollars, ad spend stays in the brand's own account, and US clients include Frank Zoller Authentic History and the Gettysburg Museum of History.

### What is Housefly by Drifted Marketing?

Drifted Marketing built Housefly to run its own studio. Most of the team works beside an AI agent that keeps its own memory, the agents trade notes through a shared hive, overnight jobs run on the studio’s own machine, and anything touching a client account waits for a human yes with a single-use code.

### What does it actually cost?

Two published monthly fees — $2,000 for one discipline, $4,000 for the full content and findability loop — or a tailored fee priced to your revenue target on the first call, out loud, before any contract exists. Advertising spend is separate. If the maths does not work for you, we will say so and point you somewhere cheaper.

### How fast until we see anything?

Work starts in week one and the first creative is live in week three. Numbers by week four. The check-in cadence is written into the contract beside the target, so you know when you will hear from us before you sign anything.

### How do we know it is working?

Every figure we report names its client and carries a receipt. The Gallery gets $5.20–$6 back per $1 of ad spend, every campaign to July 2026. That is published, not claimed — and where a number is not measured yet, the page says pending rather than guessing.

### Is the AI work snake oil?

Sometimes, elsewhere. Here it is a typist with perfect stamina: 1,250 auction listings written from photographs, 400+ hours returned to a real team, every listing checked by a person. The machine does volume; people do judgement.

### What if we want out?

Thirty days’ notice. You keep everything we made — files, accounts, ad history, the lot. If the work does not hold you, a clause should not have to.

### Are we too small for you?

The Poster Project had 811 followers at the time and reached 2.2M views in ninety days, 80% of it organic. Size is not the test. A clear number and a date are, and the founder signs off both on the first call.

### Who actually does the work?

The people in the studio photograph. There is no account layer and no handoff to someone junior at signature. When you call, a person who touched your work answers — that is structural, not a promise.

### Why “Drifted”?

Because we drifted from how agencies are supposed to run — the theatre, the bloat, the invented metrics — and kept only the craft. The name is the pitch; the site is the evidence.

### Can a Karachi agency work New York hours?

Yes — it is how we work. Drifted's team is in Karachi and works the New York business day, so you message during your day and hear back during your day. You never wait for Karachi to wake up, and the calls sit in your calendar, not ours.

### Do you build AI apps for small businesses in Pakistan?

We do. Drifted builds custom AI apps scoped to one business's real workload. Ehsaan, a person-to-person thrift marketplace app for Pakistan, reached its first build in 23 prompts; the listing platform we built for Frank Zoller Authentic History writes auction listings from photographs and has saved 400+ hours. How a tool earns is decided before any code is written.

### Do you work with brands in the United States?

Yes. The team keeps New York hours from Karachi, so a US brand gets a same-day partner rather than an overnight one. In the United States we work with Frank Zoller Authentic History and the Gettysburg Museum of History; in the Netherlands, with Oorlogsspullen, a militaria shop; in Pakistan, with The Gallery and ehsaan.

### What happens on the first call?

Thirty minutes, no deck. You bring the number you need to hit and the date; we tell you on the call whether we can, what it would cost and what we would do first. If the answer is no, you hear that too, along with where we would go instead.

# The journal, in full — written by Umer Tariq

## Shopify SEO: the fixes that actually matter for a small store

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/shopify-seo-the-fixes-that-matter/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-28

What Shopify already does for search, the handful of settings and pages it leaves to you, and the app habits that quietly slow a store down.

Shopify does more for search out of the box than most store owners realise, and that is part of the problem: it is easy to assume it does everything. The stores that never appear on Google usually have the same handful of gaps, none of them technical, all of them fixable in an afternoon each.

**The short version.** Shopify already builds the sitemap, the robots file and canonical links for you. What it leaves to you is the words: a unique title and description for every product and collection, product descriptions written for a buyer rather than copied from a supplier, image alt text, collection pages with a paragraph of real copy, and fewer apps. Do those, connect Search Console, and most small stores are ahead of their competitors.

### What does Shopify handle on its own?

- A sitemap of products, collections, pages and blog posts, kept up to date at the store's own address.
- A robots file that keeps the cart, checkout and account pages out of search.
- Canonical links, so a product reached through several collections counts as one page.
- Basic structured data in most current themes, so Google can read price and availability.

### What does it leave to you?

| Fix | Where in Shopify | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product titles and descriptions for search | Each product's search engine listing | Shopify fills them from the product name and first lines, which rarely match what buyers type |
| Original product descriptions | The product page | Supplier copy appears on hundreds of stores; Google shows one |
| Image alt text | Each product image | Image search, and a description for anyone using a screen reader |
| Collection page copy | Each collection | A grid of products with no words gives Google nothing to rank |
| Clean handles | The URL field | Short, readable addresses, set before launch, not changed after |
| Redirects | Navigation, URL redirects | When a product is deleted, its address should point somewhere useful |

### Why are collection pages the biggest opportunity?

Because buyers search for categories far more often than for a single product: "linen bedding", "newborn gift set", "leather wallet for men". The page that should rank for those is a collection. Give each one a clear title, a short paragraph at the top saying what is in it and who it suits, and a few answered questions at the bottom. That turns a grid into a page Google can understand.

### How do apps hurt Shopify SEO?

Each app tends to add its own scripts to every page, and an uninstalled app often leaves its code behind in the theme. The result is a slower store, and speed on a phone is both a ranking signal and a sales problem. Audit the apps every few months, remove the ones nobody uses, and check the theme for leftovers after each removal.

### How do you see whether it is working?

Connect Google Search Console and submit the sitemap. Within a few weeks it shows which searches the store appears for, which pages Google has indexed and which it has skipped and why. Read it once a month: the searches where you appear but nobody clicks are the titles and descriptions to rewrite first.

### How do we do it?

On Starter's search option, at $2,000 a month, we take four pages a month through exactly this list, write one researched article and keep the Google Business listing active if the store has a door. On Standard, at $4,000, the search work sits beside the ads and the content, so the pages the ads send people to are the same ones built to be found.

### When will SEO not help a Shopify store?

When nobody searches for what it sells yet. A new kind of product, or a brand people only discover by seeing it, will get more from short video and ads that create the demand. Search catches demand that already exists; it rarely creates it.

## Getting a Karachi cafe or restaurant found on Google Maps

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/getting-a-karachi-cafe-found-on-google-maps/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-28

The listing settings, photographs, menus and reviews that decide whether a hungry person in Karachi finds your place or the one next door.

In Karachi, a decision about where to eat tonight is usually made on a phone, on Google Maps or Instagram, in the minute before someone gets into the car. The places that win that minute are not always the best ones. They are the ones whose listing answers every question before it is asked.

**The short version.** Claim and verify the Google Business Profile, pick the most exact category, and keep hours, phone and WhatsApp correct. Add a real menu, recent photographs of the food and the room, and the attributes people filter on, such as delivery, outdoor seating and family seating. Post weekly, reply to every review, and make sure the name and address match Instagram and Foodpanda exactly.

### What decides which cafes show up first?

Google says it ranks local results on relevance, distance and prominence. Distance you cannot change. Relevance comes from the category, the menu and the words in the listing. Prominence comes from reviews, photographs, mentions elsewhere and how active the listing is. A complete listing that posts and replies regularly will often outrank a better restaurant a street away whose listing was claimed once and forgotten.

| Setting | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Primary category | The most exact one: Cafe, Pizza restaurant, Barbecue restaurant, not just Restaurant |
| Hours | Including late-night hours and Ramadan timings, changed before the day, not after |
| Phone and WhatsApp | A number someone answers during opening hours |
| Menu | Real items and prices, updated when they change |
| Attributes | Delivery, takeaway, dine-in, outdoor seating, family area, parking |
| Photographs | The food, the room, the front door at night, so people recognise it |

### What should a restaurant post?

One post a week is enough if it is real: a new dish, a deal for a match night, a change in timings. Short video made for Instagram can be reused here. The point is not volume; it is showing Google and the customer that the place is open, active and worth the drive.

### How do you get more good reviews?

Ask at the right moment: a card on the table with the bill, or a message after a delivery that arrived hot. Never buy reviews or trade them for a free dessert; Google removes them and can suspend the listing, and a suspended listing in a busy area is a disaster. Reply to every review, and to the angry ones calmly and specifically. The next customer reads the reply, not the complaint.

### Why do Instagram and Foodpanda matter to Google?

Because they confirm who you are. When the name, address and phone read the same on the Google listing, Instagram, Foodpanda and any food guide, both Google and the AI assistants that answer "best cafe in DHA" can be confident they are looking at one place. When they disagree, you look like two businesses, and neither is trusted.

### What does this cost to have done?

Claiming and filling in the listing is free and an owner can do it in an afternoon. Where we come in is keeping it alive alongside the rest: Starter's search option at $2,000 a month covers page optimisations, a researched article and Google Business posts every month, and the content option covers short videos and carousels for Instagram. Our studio is in DHA Phase 8, so the first call can be in person.

### When is this not worth paying for?

When the place is already full every night and the problem is the kitchen, not the queue. Search brings people to the door; it cannot bring them back a second time. Fix the food and the service first, and spend on being found when there are empty tables to fill.

## What app development costs with an offshore team

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/app-development-cost-with-an-offshore-team/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-28

What actually drives the price of an app built offshore, the costs that do not show up in the quote, and the contract terms that protect a startup.

Founders look offshore for one reason: the same budget buys more building. That is true, and it is also where the trouble starts, because a lower day rate on a badly scoped project is still an expensive project. The cost of an app is set far more by what you ask for, and how clearly, than by where the team sits.

**The short version.** An app's cost is driven by scope first: how many kinds of user, whether money moves through it, how many platforms, and what it connects to. An offshore team lowers the rate, not the scope. The hidden costs are time-zone delay, rework from a loose brief, and code you do not own. Fix all three in the contract: overlapping hours, a written scope tied to how the app earns, and the code in your own account from day one.

### What drives the cost of an app?

| Driver | Cheaper end | Dearer end |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kinds of user | One | Buyers, sellers and an admin |
| Money | None, or a link out | Payments, payouts, refunds |
| Platforms | One, or a web app | iPhone, Android and web |
| Connections | None | Maps, messaging, outside data |
| Trust features | None | Identity checks, reviews, reporting |
| Content | Fixed | Uploaded by users, needing moderation |

### Fixed price or time and materials?

A fixed price suits a narrow, well-defined first version: the builder carries the risk of overrun, and you carry the risk that the scope was wrong. Time and materials suits a product that will change as you learn, but it needs a weekly view of hours and progress or it drifts. A sensible middle path is a fixed price for a written first version and a monthly retainer after launch.

### What costs do not show up in the quote?

- Store accounts: Apple's developer programme charges a yearly fee and Google Play a one-time fee, both in your name.
- Hosting, databases, email sending, maps and other paid services, billed monthly as the app grows.
- Maintenance: operating system updates break things every year, and someone has to fix them.
- Your own time: answering questions, testing builds and making decisions. A slow answer stalls a fast team.
- Rework when the brief said one thing and meant another.

### Does the time zone matter?

More than the rate. A team that sleeps through your working day turns every question into a day's delay, and a project with many small questions loses weeks that way. Ask for a few hours of overlap at minimum, or a team that works your hours outright. Our studio is in Karachi and works New York business hours, precisely so a founder in the United States gets answers the same afternoon.

### What should the contract say?

1. The code, the design files and every account are yours from the first day, in repositories and stores you own.
2. A written scope for the first version, tied to how the app earns money.
3. What happens to bugs found after launch, and for how long.
4. Who the named people on the project are, and that they cannot be swapped silently.
5. Thirty days' notice either way, with a clean handover.

### How do we price a build?

Per build, under our Tailored tier, to the number the app is meant to produce, because a marketplace with payments and trust features is not the same project as a booking tool for one clinic. For ehsaan, a person-to-person marketplace app for Pakistan, we wrote a 19-section knowledge base before building and reached the first build in 23 prompts. The revenue model is written before the first screen, and the client keeps the code.

### When is offshore the wrong call?

When the founder cannot write down what the first version must do, or has no time to answer questions each week. Distance magnifies vagueness. In that case, spend first on a short paid scoping exercise, wherever the team is, and only then decide who builds it.

## What is GEO, and does a small business need it?

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/what-is-geo-and-does-a-small-business-need-it/ · How we work · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-28

Generative engine optimisation in plain English, what it shares with ordinary search work, and the short list of things a small business should actually do.

Every few years search gets a new acronym and a new invoice line. Generative engine optimisation, written GEO, is the current one. The question a small business owner should ask is not what it stands for but whether it is a different job from the search work they may already be paying for. Mostly, it is not.

**The short version.** Generative engine optimisation is the work of being named and cited when an AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini or Google's AI summaries answers a question. Most of it is good search engine optimisation done to a stricter standard: pages that answer the question first, a business described the same way everywhere, and listings and reviews that back it up. A small business rarely needs it as a separate service; it needs its search work done that way.

### What is generative engine optimisation?

Search engines return a list of links. Assistants write an answer and, increasingly, name the sources they drew it from. Generative engine optimisation is everything that makes your business one of those sources: being easy to find, easy to understand and easy to quote, and being described consistently enough that the assistant is confident you are who you say you are.

### How is it different from SEO?

|  | Search engine optimisation | Generative engine optimisation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you win | A place in a list of links | A mention or a citation inside an answer |
| What it reads | Pages, links, listings | The same, plus reviews and directory profiles |
| What it rewards | Relevance and authority | Clear answers, consistency and corroboration |
| How you measure it | Search Console, in Google's own data | Asking the assistants and writing down what they say |

### What should a small business actually do?

1. Open each important page with a direct answer to the question it exists for, in two or three plain sentences.
2. Describe the business in one sentence, and use that same sentence on the website, the Google listing, and every directory and social profile.
3. Keep name, address and phone identical everywhere, character for character.
4. Publish the facts an assistant gets asked for: what you sell, where, for whom, and roughly what it costs.
5. Earn reviews and mentions on sites the assistants already trust in your field.
6. Every month, ask the assistants the questions a buyer would, and note who they name.

### Is llms.txt worth adding?

It is a plain-text file at a fixed address on a website that states, in order, who the business is, what it sells and where the proof is. It is a proposed convention, not a standard every assistant has said it reads. It takes an hour to write and costs nothing to keep, so we add one, ours included, and treat it as cheap insurance rather than a ranking lever.

### Can anyone guarantee an AI citation?

No. Assistants change their answers from week to week and from one way of asking to another. An agency promising that ChatGPT will recommend you is selling something it does not control. What it can promise is the work above, done well, and a monthly record of what the assistants actually say.

### How do we handle it?

As one piece of work with search, not three. Starter's search option is $2,000 a month: page optimisations, a researched article and Google Business posts. Standard, at $4,000, adds the answer-engine work and a monthly record of what the assistants say about you. We do not publish a figure for how often assistants cite us, because we have not measured it to a standard we would defend.

### When does a small business not need it at all?

When nearly all its customers come from walking past, from word of mouth or from one marketplace. A corner bakery needs a complete Google listing and good reviews, which serve both search and assistants, and very little else. Spend on this when buyers research before they buy, and ask an assistant while they do.

## How to get a museum on Google Maps

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/how-to-get-a-museum-on-google-maps/ · Creator growth · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-28

Claiming the listing, the category that matters, hours and events, photographs of the collection, and the reviews that bring visitors through the door.

A visitor deciding what to do this weekend rarely starts on a museum's website. They type "museums near me" or the name of the town into Google, and the answer is a map with a few listings under it. If the museum is not there, or is there with the wrong hours, it has lost the visit before anyone read a word it wrote.

**The short version.** Claim the museum's Google Business Profile, verify it, set the primary category to Museum, and fill in everything: hours including holidays, the address, the website, the phone, photographs of the building and the collection. Post events as they come, answer every review, and keep it current. Google ranks local listings on relevance, distance and prominence, and a complete, active listing wins on the two a museum controls.

### How do you add or claim a museum on Google Maps?

1. Search for the museum on Google Maps. If a listing exists, open it and choose the option to claim or manage it. If not, add the place from Google Business Profile.
2. Verify ownership. Google offers a method per business, often a short video of the building and the signage, sometimes a phone call or a postcard.
3. Set the primary category to Museum, or the more exact one if it fits, such as History museum or Art museum. Add secondary categories only where true.
4. Fill in the rest: hours, special hours for holidays and closures, the website, a phone number answered during opening hours, and accessibility details.
5. Give the listing to an account the museum owns, with a second manager added, so it does not leave with one person.

### What does Google use to rank a museum in Maps?

Google's own guidance names three things: relevance, meaning how well the listing matches the search; distance from the searcher; and prominence, meaning how well known the place is, which reviews, links and articles about it feed. A museum cannot move itself closer to a visitor, but it can make the listing complete and accurate, and it can earn reviews and mentions.

| What to fill in | Why it matters for a museum |
| --- | --- |
| Primary category | Decides which searches the museum can appear for at all |
| Hours and holiday hours | Wrong hours earn the worst reviews a museum gets |
| Photographs of the collection | The object is what makes someone choose to come |
| Event posts | Exhibitions and anniversaries give people a reason to come now |
| Review replies | Show the listing is watched, and answer the next visitor's question |
| Website link to a real visit page | Sends people to tickets and directions, not the home page |

### What should a museum post?

The collection, one object at a time, with a line on why it matters, and every event with its date. A post about a new exhibition, a lecture or an anniversary weekend gives the listing fresh activity and gives a searcher a reason to visit this week rather than someday. The same photographs and lines can feed the museum's social accounts; the object is the content everywhere.

### How should a museum handle reviews?

Ask for them at the moment a visit goes well: a card at the desk, a line at the end of a tour. Never pay for them or trade them for a discount; Google removes those and can penalise the listing. Answer every review, the bad ones first and calmly. A reply that explains the parking or the closing time helps the next visitor more than the person who complained.

### What have we done for a museum?

Our search work for the Gettysburg Museum of History in Pennsylvania included repairing the museum's listing, an event page for its October anniversary weekend and the Foundation's new site, written so people searching for the weekend landed on the museum's own page. No figure is published for it yet, and we would rather say so than invent one.

### When does a museum not need outside help with this?

When someone on staff has an hour a week and will keep doing it. Claiming and filling in the listing is free and needs no agency. Outside help earns its fee when the listing is part of a larger push, such as an exhibition launch with films, posts and a page built to be found, or when nobody inside has the time.

## What a Shopify store costs in Pakistan

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/what-a-shopify-store-costs-in-pakistan/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-28

Every line item in a Pakistani Shopify store, which ones are fixed by Shopify and which ones a developer sets, and how to read a quote.

Ask three developers in Karachi what a Shopify store costs and you will get three numbers that cannot be compared, because each one prices a different store. The honest answer is a list, not a figure: a handful of costs Shopify sets and you cannot negotiate, and a handful a developer sets that you can.

**The short version.** A Shopify store in Pakistan has two kinds of cost. Running costs are set by others: Shopify's monthly plan, billed in dollars, any paid apps, a domain, and payment and courier fees. Build costs are set by whoever makes it: the theme, the setup, the product pages and the photographs. Get every quote broken into those lines, and the cheapest one usually turns out to be missing one.

### What does Shopify itself charge?

A monthly plan fee, billed in US dollars to a card, with a cheaper rate if you pay for the year up front. The plans and prices are on Shopify's own pricing page, and Shopify adjusts them by country, so read that page from Pakistan rather than trusting a figure in an old blog post. Most small stores start on the lowest plan and only move up when staff accounts or reporting demand it.

### How do payments work for a store in Pakistan?

Shopify's own card processing, Shopify Payments, is not offered to businesses in Pakistan. So a store here either connects a local payment gateway or takes cash on delivery, and most do both. Each gateway charges its own fee per transaction, and Shopify adds a small fee of its own on orders paid through an outside gateway. Cash on delivery costs nothing to switch on, but it brings returns and refused parcels, which are a real cost even if no invoice shows them.

| Line item | Who sets it | Paid how |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shopify plan | Shopify | Monthly, in dollars |
| Theme | Theme maker, or free | Once |
| Apps | Each app's maker | Mostly monthly |
| Domain | Domain registrar | Yearly |
| Payment gateway | The gateway | Per order |
| Courier and returns | The courier | Per parcel |
| Setup and product pages | Your developer | Once |
| Photographs | Your photographer | Per shoot |

### What does a developer charge for, and what is it worth?

The build: choosing and setting up the theme, connecting the gateway and the courier, writing the product pages, setting shipping rules for cash on delivery, and making the checkout work on a cheap phone on a slow connection, because that is where most Pakistani orders are placed. A free theme set up well beats a paid theme set up badly. The part worth paying for is the product page: the words and pictures that make a stranger trust a store they found ten seconds ago.

### Why do apps quietly double the bill?

Because each one is cheap on its own and billed monthly forever. Reviews, upsells, a WhatsApp button, a size chart, a currency switcher: a store can collect a dozen in its first year, each adding to the bill and to the page's load time. Before installing one, ask whether the theme already does it. Most good themes do more than their owners know.

### How do we price a store?

We price a store build and its photography per project, under our Tailored tier, because a ten-product store and a store with hundreds of variants are different amounts of work. The ads that send people to it are Starter's ads option at $2,000 a month, with the spend separate and in your own account. Every account, the store, the domain and the ad account, is in your name from the first day.

### What should a quote include?

- Every running cost you will pay after launch, listed, not just the build fee.
- Which apps it assumes, and what each one costs a month.
- Who owns the store, the domain and the theme licence when the work ends. It should be you.
- How the checkout handles cash on delivery and a local gateway together.
- Who writes the product pages and who takes the photographs.

### When is Shopify the wrong choice?

When almost every sale closes in Instagram messages and is paid in cash at the door. A store then mostly serves as a catalogue, and a well-kept Instagram account with a clear order process may do the same job for less. Build the store when buyers want to check out without talking to anyone, or when the ads need a page to send people to.

## How a small agency runs AI agents safely: the human yes

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/running-ai-agents-safely-the-human-yes/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-27

Why an agent should propose but never approve, how an approval gate with a single-use code works, and the other rules that make an agent safe to trust with a client.

The fastest way to lose a client with AI is to let an agent change their account on its own. A paused campaign, an edited order or a message sent in the wrong tone takes seconds to do and weeks to repair. The answer is not to keep agents away from real work. It is to build the pause into the system so it cannot be skipped.

**The short version.** Let the agent read, prepare and propose. Never let it approve. Anything that would change a client's live account should stop at one gate, state its consequence in a plain sentence, and run only when a person approves it with a single-use code. Record who decided, remember every no, and keep credentials where the agent cannot reach them.

### Why should an agent not act on its own?

Because the agent that suggests an action should never be the one that signs it off. Agents are fast and confident, and they read text written by other people, some of it written to mislead an assistant. A person in the loop is not a formality. It is the part of the system that knows the client.

### What is an approval gate?

One chokepoint that every consequential action passes through. The list of action kinds is closed, so adding a new one is a code change a person reviews. Reading runs freely. Writing has to be armed and approved.

1. The agent proposes. It can describe the action. It cannot approve it and cannot run it.
2. The gate arms it. It writes, in one plain sentence, exactly what will happen, and issues a single-use code.
3. A person approves. Nothing runs until the approval comes back quoting that exact code, so the pause is enforced by the software and not drawn on a screen.
4. The decision is recorded. Every yes and every no names who made it.
5. A no is remembered. The agent cannot reopen a rejected question by asking it again in different words.

### What should never be automatic?

| Kind of action | Rule | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reading numbers, messages and calls | Free, read-only | Looking cannot change anything |
| Changing a client's account | Proposed, armed, approved | Mistakes reach the client |
| Sending a call's words for summary | Its own approved action | It sends a client's words off the machine |
| Acting on another agent's note | Only with your own person's yes | A note is information, not an order |

### How do you keep credentials away from the agent?

Do not rely on telling it not to look. Matching words in a command is not enough, because a path can be assembled in pieces across several harmless-looking steps. Have the operating system refuse the agent's shell access to the credential files outright, however the request is spelled. If that layer is ever missing, the system should say so out loud rather than carry on quietly.

### What about instructions hidden in what the agent reads?

Treat everything the agent reads as information, never instruction: a web page, a transcript, an email, a note from another agent. Any of them can carry a line written to an assistant. The approval gate is the backstop. Even if a hidden line talks an agent into proposing something, a person still has to approve it.

### What other rules are worth having?

- Partial success is failure. A job that finished most of its work did not finish, and the record should say what failed.
- Filters fail closed. If a safety check cannot run, the answer is no.
- Briefs say what they could not read. A summary built on stale data and presented as current is worse than none.
- No setting switches the gate off. A control that can be disabled will be, on the busiest day of the year.

### Does all this slow the team down?

Less than you would think. The agent still does the reading, the preparation and the drafting, which is most of the time. The person spends a moment on the decision that matters. That is the right split: the agent multiplies the team, and the team keeps the judgement it was hired for.

### How do we run it?

Exactly this way. Housefly, the system we built to run Drifted, gives most of the team an agent of their own, and every action that would touch a client's live account waits at one gate for a person's yes with a single-use code. There is no setting to turn it off. It is being prepared for a public release.

### When is a gate overkill?

When nothing the agent touches can reach a client or cost money: drafting internal notes, tidying files, summarising your own reading. Gate the writes that leave the building, and let the rest run.

## What an AI agent with memory actually does for a small team

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/ai-agent-with-memory-for-a-small-team/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-27

What memory means for an AI agent, what it changes in a small team's day, why each person should have their own, and what goes wrong.

Most people meet AI as a chat window that forgets them the moment it closes. That is useful for a one-off question and close to useless for running a business, where the value is in everything that happened before today. An agent with memory is the difference between a clever stranger and a colleague who was in the room last week.

**The short version.** Memory turns an AI assistant from a tool you brief every time into a colleague that already knows how you work. For a small team the gain is not replacing people; it is multiplying them. The agent reads, remembers, chases and drafts, and the people keep the taste, the judgement and the client.

### What does memory mean for an AI agent?

It means written notes the agent reads before it answers: corrections it has been given, decisions that were made, and how its person likes the work done. It is not the model quietly retraining itself. It is closer to a well-kept notebook, which is good news, because a notebook can be read, corrected and audited by a person.

|  | A chat assistant | An agent with memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Each morning | Starts from nothing | Starts from what it learned |
| A correction | Needed every time | Given once, written down |
| Context on a client | Pasted in by you | Already filed under that client |
| Who it works for | Whoever is typing | One named person |

### What does it change in a small team's day?

The work that eats a small team is rarely the hard part. It is the reading before a call, the notes after it, the promise someone made and nobody wrote down, the report assembled by hand at the end of the month. That is exactly the work an agent with memory is good at.

- Before a call: a brief from the client's recent messages, numbers and calls, saying which sources it actually managed to read.
- After a call: the notes split into what we owe the client and what the client owes us, with each promise tracked until it is done.
- At the end of the month: the report drafted from the numbers, with the part about what to do next left for a person.
- Overnight: scheduled checks and tidying, so the results are waiting in the morning.

### Does it replace anyone?

Not in a team that is run well. The expertise in a studio is its people: the eye for what will work, the judgement on a client's account, the trust on a call. An agent cannot hold any of that. What it can do is clear the ground around it, so each person spends more of the day on the part only they can do. Think of it as multiplying the team rather than shrinking it.

### Why should each person have their own agent?

Because memory is personal. An editor and a salesperson want different things remembered, in different words. One shared assistant for the whole company ends up remembering everything for nobody. An agent per person learns one way of working and answers to one person, which also makes it clear who decides what it does.

### How do the agents share what they know?

Through a shared space where they leave each other notes and offer each other tasks. The rules matter more than the plumbing. A note from another agent is information, never an order. A task is an offer that waits until its person accepts it in their own words. And only what a person marks as shared ever leaves their machine.

### What goes wrong with agent memory?

- Stale notes. A ruling from last month can outlive the decision that reversed it. The fix is a plain rule: when two notes disagree, the later date wins, and the agent says which one it followed.
- Confident errors. An agent that remembers a wrong fact repeats it with conviction. Notes must be easy for a person to read and correct.
- Leaks between clients. A note about one client must never reach another client's brief. File memory by client and by project from the start.
- Secrets in memory. Passwords and keys never belong in notes. Scan anything shared before it travels, and refuse to send if the scan cannot run.

### What does this look like in practice?

We run it. Housefly is the system we built for our own studio: most people at Drifted work beside an agent of their own, the agents pass notes through a shared hive, and overnight work runs on the studio's own machine. It was built by our founder, the team uses it every day, and it is being prepared for a public release.

### When is an agent with memory not worth it?

When the work does not repeat. If every week is genuinely different and nothing carries over, memory has little to hold, and a good chat assistant used well is enough. It earns its keep where the same clients, the same reports and the same kinds of call come round again and again.

## What a personal-brand website costs

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/what-a-personal-brand-website-costs/ · Creator growth · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-27

What moves the price of a website for a coach, healer or creator, what you should own at the end, and the running costs nobody mentions in the quote.

Quotes for a personal-brand website vary so widely that the numbers are close to useless on their own. What makes them comparable is knowing what drives the price and what you own when it is done. This piece names the drivers, so you can read any quote, ours included, line by line.

**The short version.** The price is set by the number of pages, who writes the words, whether you take bookings or payments, and how custom the design is. The domain and hosting are running costs, and they must be in your name. Ask every quote what is included, what is not, and what you can change yourself afterwards.

### What drives the cost of a personal-brand website?

| Driver | Cheaper | Dearer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pages | A handful, one per offering | Many, with articles and events |
| Words | You write them | Written for you from your material |
| Bookings and payments | A contact form | A calendar, payments, courses or memberships |
| Design | A good template, well set up | A custom look built for you |
| Photography | Your own photographs | A shoot |

### What are the running costs?

- The domain, renewed every year.
- Hosting, monthly or yearly, depending on the platform.
- Any booking, payment or email tool, usually by subscription.
- Changes you cannot make yourself, if the site was built without a way for you to edit it.

### What should you own at the end?

Everything: the domain, the hosting account, the site, the words and the photographs, in your name from the start. A site held in a designer's account is a site you rent. Ask before you pay who the domain is registered to.

### How do we price it?

Per build, under the Tailored tier on our pricing page, with the figure given before anything is built. Channeling with Emily, a site for a medium and healer in California, was quoted as one figure before work began, and is in final review. The studio is in Karachi and keeps New York hours, which suits clients in the United States, overlaps the afternoon for clients in the Netherlands and Europe, and puts us a short drive away for clients in Pakistan.

### Do you need a website before you have an audience?

You need one before the audience arrives, which can be sooner than you expect. The Poster Project, the founder's own brand, reached 2.2M views in 90 days from a small account, most of them organic. Reach comes before followers, and a visitor who arrives from a post that travelled needs somewhere to land.

### When is a cheaper route better?

When you are still testing what you offer. A site builder and an afternoon of writing will tell you whether people get in touch. Pay for a built site when the offerings are settled and the site is costing you clients by being unclear.

## What a website for a coach or healer needs

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/website-for-a-coach-or-healer/ · Creator growth · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-27

The pages, the words and the contact setup that turn a recommendation into a first session, for coaches, healers, mediums and anyone whose business is themselves.

A coach or a healer is usually found by name. Someone hears about you from a friend, a talk or a post, and searches for you to check you are real and to see what you offer. The website's job is to answer that visitor quickly, in your own voice, and make the first contact easy. Everything else is optional.

**The short version.** Four pages: who you help, what you offer, who you are, how to reach you. Write them in the words you use with clients. Give each offering its own page with what happens in a session. Use a simple contact form unless your diary is fixed. Answer the questions a first-time client is too shy to ask.

### Which pages does a coach or healer need?

| Page | What it must answer |
| --- | --- |
| Home | Who you help, with what, and how to start |
| Each offering | What happens, how long it takes, online or in person, and how to ask |
| About | How you came to this work, told plainly and truthfully |
| Contact | One easy way to reach you, and when you reply |
| Questions | What first-time clients wonder but rarely ask |

### Should the site have online booking?

Only if your diary is fixed enough to keep it honest. A practitioner who travels, or who prefers to speak to someone before booking them, is better served by a contact form and a prompt reply. Channeling with Emily, a website we built for a psychic medium and healer in California, uses a contact form rather than a booking calendar for exactly that reason. It is in final review.

### How should the words be written?

In your own voice, from your own material. Your bio, a recording of a talk, the way you explain a session to a nervous first-timer: these are better raw material than anything a template offers. Keep the claims to what you can stand behind. Say what a session involves and how clients describe feeling afterwards, rather than promising outcomes.

### How do people find a coach or healer by search?

Two ways. By name, which needs only a site that loads fast and says the same thing as your social profiles. And by question: what is a reading, what happens in a healing session, can it be done online. A short page answering each question in plain words is what both search engines and AI assistants quote.

### What changes between the US, Europe and Pakistan?

- In the United States, say plainly whether sessions are online, in person or both, and in which state.
- In the Netherlands and the rest of the European Union, a contact form collects personal data, so publish a short privacy note saying what you keep and why.
- In Pakistan, many clients will reach you on WhatsApp before they use a form, so put the number where they can find it.

### When is hiring a studio the wrong call?

When you are still finding out what you offer. A simple page on a site builder, written in your own words, is enough to test whether people book. Hire help when the offerings are settled and the site is what stands between a recommendation and a first session.

## How to hire app developers for a startup

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/how-to-hire-app-developers-for-a-startup/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-27

Freelancer, in-house or a studio, onshore or offshore: how to choose, what to put in the contract, and the questions that expose a bad fit before you pay for one.

Most early startups do not need a development team. They need a working first version in front of real users, built so that whoever comes next can continue it. Hiring for that is a different job from hiring a team to maintain a product at scale, and most of the expensive mistakes come from confusing the two.

**The short version.** Before a working first version, hire a small studio or one strong freelancer, not a team. Put the repository and every account in your name from the first day. Write the product's rules down before the screens. Ask to see a live build with the client named or described. Choose by how fast they answer and how plainly they scope, not by the length of the proposal.

### Freelancer, in-house or studio?

| Option | Good when | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One freelancer | The scope is small and you can review the code | One person is a single point of failure |
| An in-house hire | The product works and needs a full-time owner | Slow to hire and costly to get wrong |
| A studio | You need the product, the design and the launch together | Ownership and continuity must be written into the contract |

### Does it matter where the developers are?

Less than it used to, as long as the hours overlap and the contract is clear. A founder in the United States hiring offshore should ask what time the studio answers messages, not where it is. A founder in the Netherlands or elsewhere in Europe often finds a studio on New York hours overlaps the afternoon well. A founder in Pakistan has a strong local market and should hold it to the same contract terms as anyone abroad. Our own studio is in Karachi and keeps New York hours for this reason.

### What should the contract say?

- The repository, hosting, domains and model keys are created in your name, not transferred at the end.
- A written scope for the first version, priced separately from the full build.
- A knowledge base or specification that a new developer could continue from.
- A notice period, and exactly what you keep when the work ends.
- Who on their side writes the code, by name.

### How fast can a first version be built?

Faster than most proposals suggest, when the rules are written first. For ehsaan, a pre-loved fashion marketplace in Pakistan, the first build took 23 prompts with AI tooling, and the product now runs against a 19-section knowledge base that records every rule it follows. The tooling made the first version fast; the knowledge base is what lets the next developer continue it.

### Questions that expose a bad fit

1. Can I see a live build, and talk to the client?
2. Whose name is the repository in today?
3. What does the first version cost, and what does the full build cost?
4. What happens to my product if you stop working with me?
5. How will you tell me the scope is wrong?

### When is a studio the wrong hire?

When the product already works and needs one person to own it every day. At that point an in-house engineer who lives with the product is worth more than any studio, ours included. A studio is for getting to a working product, or for building the parts a small team does not have time for.

## How to sell militaria online

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/how-to-sell-militaria-online/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-27

Where to sell, how to write a listing a collector trusts, how to price from realised sales, and what changes between the US, the Netherlands and the rest of Europe.

Militaria sells to the most exacting buyers in collecting. A collector knows the maker's marks, the period variations and the fakes better than most sellers do, and they buy on the description before they buy on the photograph. Selling online is less about finding a platform than about writing listings that survive that reader. We work with an auction house in the United States and a militaria shop in the Netherlands, and the lessons below come from both.

**The short version.** Pick the channel by the value of the piece: auction for rare items, your own shop for steady stock, marketplaces only where their rules allow the category. Write every listing with the maker, the period, the marks, the condition and the provenance, in that order. Price from realised sales, not asking prices. Photograph the marks as carefully as the front. Then build a list of collectors you can write to directly.

### Where should you sell militaria online?

| Channel | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specialist auction house | Rare and high-value pieces with a known market | Commission, consignment timelines, and the catalogue deadline |
| Your own online shop | Steady stock sold between sales, repeat collectors | You bring the traffic; nobody else does |
| General marketplaces | Lower-value pieces and wide reach | Restricted-item rules that remove listings without warning |
| Collector forums and groups | Specialist items and trusted sellers | Trades on reputation; no buyer protection by default |

Most dealers end up using two of these. An auction calendar sells the rare pieces at their best price; a shop of your own sells the rest between sales and keeps the collectors who found you at auction.

### What makes a militaria listing trustworthy?

Specific facts in a fixed order. A collector scans for the same things every time, and a listing that puts them where the eye expects them reads as a seller who knows the field.

1. The item, the nation and the period, in the title.
2. The maker and every mark, with a photograph of each.
3. The condition, stated plainly, flaws first.
4. The provenance: where it came from, and what paperwork goes with it.
5. What you do not know, said outright. A collector trusts a seller who admits a gap more than one who fills it with guesses.

### How do you price militaria?

From what comparable pieces actually sold for, not what other sellers are asking. Asking prices on a marketplace tell you what people hope for; realised prices at auction tell you what collectors paid. If you have your own sales history, it is the best reference you own. The auction house we work with loaded its past items into the system that now drafts its listings, so every new lot is written and estimated against its own record.

### How do you write listings faster without losing accuracy?

Write from photographs and your own history, and review only what is uncertain. For the US auction house, every sale meant 1,250 lots typed by hand. We built a platform that reads the photographs, drafts each listing from a 32,000-item reference set and flags only the lots it is unsure of for a person to check. It went live for the auction of 16 August and has taken 400+ hours off the client's desk. For the shop in the Netherlands, an AI writer drafts each product listing and the dealer corrects and publishes it.

### What changes between the US, the Netherlands and the rest of Europe?

- In the United States, the collector market is large and auction-led, and most bidding platforms take a catalogue upload in their own template.
- In the Netherlands and elsewhere in Europe, some countries restrict the public display or sale of certain symbols and insignia. Check the law where you sell and where you ship before you list.
- Shipping out of the European Union, or into it from the United States, means customs paperwork. Say in the listing who pays duties.
- Whatever the country, marketplaces apply their own restricted-item rules on top of the law, and they change them without notice.

### When is hiring help the wrong call?

When your stock is small enough to describe yourself in an evening. A writing system pays when the typing is the bottleneck: hundreds of lots a sale, or a back room of photographed stock waiting for words. A dealer with a dozen pieces a month should write them personally, build a list of collectors, and spend the money on better photographs.

## AI search for a Karachi business

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/ai-search-for-a-karachi-business/ · How we work · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

Where a Karachi customer actually looks, why the Business Profile comes first, the one-name-one-address rule, the pages an assistant will quote, and what to do if you sell in DMs and take cash at the door.

A Karachi customer looking for what you sell no longer types a phrase and reads ten links. They open Maps and look at the pin. They search Instagram for the product and judge the profile in seconds. They ask a friend on WhatsApp. And, more every month, they ask an assistant and read the one answer it gives. If your business is not in that answer, it does not matter how good the feed is. This is what to do about it, for a business that may never have had a website at all.

**The short version.** Fix the Google Business Profile first, because it is the page a Karachi customer sees before any other. Use one name, one address and one phone number, spelled identically everywhere. Put the answers to the questions people ask you in DMs on pages of your own, in plain sentences, with the price and the delivery terms stated. An assistant cannot read your inbox or your pinned post; it can read a page.

### Where does a Karachi customer actually look?

In four places, and they are not the four an agency usually optimises.

- Maps and the Business Profile. For anything with a door, a cafe, a clinic, a tailor, a showroom, the search happens on the map and the decision is made on the listing: open now, how far, what it looks like, what people said.
- Instagram search and the profile. For anything sold by post or by rider, the customer searches the product, lands on a profile, and judges it on the bio, the highlights and the pinned post before sending a message.
- WhatsApp. The forward from a friend is the most trusted search result in the city, and it usually carries a screenshot of one of the above.
- The assistants. ChatGPT, Google's AI answers and the rest, asked: where do I get this, who does that in Clifton, is this shop genuine. The answer names a handful of businesses, and it names them from what it can read.

The first three a Karachi business already knows about. The fourth is new, and it is built on the same material as the first: whatever is written down about you, consistently, somewhere a machine can read it.

### Why does the Business Profile come first?

Because it is the one page about your business that Google writes into the map, into search and into its own AI answers, and most Karachi businesses have never claimed it, or claimed it once and let it rot. A profile with the wrong hours, an old phone number and three photographs of the signboard is worse than none, because the customer trusts it and is let down at the door.

Claim it. Set the category to the thing you actually sell, not the broadest thing you could. Put the hours in and keep them true through Ramazan and Eid, when every listing in the city goes wrong at once. Add photographs of the product, the inside and the people, not the sign. Answer the questions that appear on it, because the answers are read by the assistant as well as the customer. Post to it from the feed a few times a month, so it is visibly alive. Ask every happy customer for a review in a message, with the link, the day the order arrives.

The Profile is the first page an assistant trusts about a local business, because it is the one Google has verified. Everything else you write is read against it.

### What is the one address, one name rule?

Your business has one name, spelled one way, one address written one way, and one phone number formatted one way, and all three are identical on the Business Profile, the Instagram bio, the Facebook page, the website footer, the delivery app, the marketplace listing and the invoice. Identical, character for character. Not the Roman Urdu spelling on one and the English on another, not a mobile number here and a landline there, not Phase Eight in one place and an abbreviation in the next.

The reason is that an assistant decides whether two mentions are the same business by matching those three things. A business that calls itself three different names across five platforms looks like three businesses to a machine, each with a third of the evidence, and none of them gets quoted.

Pick the name today. Write the address once, as the post office would, and paste it everywhere. It is the cheapest search work there is, and in Karachi it is almost never done.

### Which pages get cited?

The page that answers one question, in the first paragraph, in sentences a machine can lift without editing. An assistant composing an answer about where to buy a thing in Karachi is looking for the page that says, plainly, what the thing is, what it costs, where it is delivered and how to order. It is not looking for a home page that welcomes you to a world.

So the pages a local business needs are the questions its inbox gets, one per page.

| The page | What it says in the first paragraph | Why an assistant quotes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What we sell | The product, who it is for, and the one thing that makes it different | It is the description the assistant will reuse |
| Prices | The price of each item, in rupees, as a plain list | A price on a page beats a price in a DM |
| Delivery | Which cities and areas, how long, what it costs, and whether cash on delivery is offered | The most asked question in Karachi, answered once |
| How to order | The steps, with the message link and the hours someone replies | The assistant can send the customer to it |
| Where we are | The address as it appears on the Profile, with the landmark | Matches the listing and confirms you are one business |
| About | Who runs it, since when, from where | Trust is a sentence with a person in it |

Each page carries the same name and address as the Profile, says what it says in the first lines, and uses headings that are the question a person would type. A site of six honest pages gets cited. A site of sixty vague ones does not.

### What if you sell in DMs, cash on delivery?

Most of Karachi does, and this is where the search work is most neglected, because the business feels it has no website to optimise. It is also where it pays most, because the assistant cannot read the one place the business has put its information. A pinned post with the price list is invisible to a machine. A highlight with the delivery areas is invisible. The saved reply that answers every question is the best-written thing the business owns, and it lives inside an inbox nobody outside can see.

The fix is to take what the saved replies already say and put it on pages. The price list becomes the prices page. The delivery reply becomes the delivery page, with cash on delivery stated plainly as a method and the terms stated beside it, because an assistant asked whether a shop does cash on delivery will quote the page that says so. The how-do-I-order reply becomes a page with the message link on it, so the assistant sends the customer into your inbox, which is where the sale was always going to close.

Nothing about the DM-first way of selling changes. The ad still starts a conversation and the sale still closes in a message. What changes is that the conversation can now begin from an answer an assistant gave, and that answer is drawn from pages you wrote rather than from whichever competitor wrote them first.

### What does Drifted do for a local business?

The work above, in order, as the search option of our Starter tier or as part of the full loop. We claim and rebuild the Business Profile and keep it posted. We list the questions the inbox gets and write a page for each, in the plain sentences an assistant can quote, with the price and the delivery terms on them. We put the one name and one address everywhere it appears and fix every place it differs.
