We add a summary file to the site written for machines to read, and we check, every month, whether the assistants are naming the business when asked the questions its customers ask.

We do the same for ourselves. This site answers each question in its first paragraph, carries one description of the studio everywhere, and publishes its fees, which is part of why it gets quoted. Two pages on it say the rest: the Karachi agency page at /pakistan/marketing-agency-karachi, which says what the fee buys for a business here, and the AI search page at /services/ai-search, which lays out the method in full.

### When is this not worth paying for?

When the business has no website and no intention of one; the Profile and the one-name rule are a morning's work the owner can do alone, and we would say so on the call. When the name changes every season, because no amount of page writing survives a business that renames itself. When nobody searches for the product at all, and the job is ads and a feed, not search. And when the owner cannot answer the inbox, because an assistant that sends a customer into an empty inbox has sent them to a competitor.

Everyone else is leaving the answer to someone else. A Karachi customer asked an assistant where to buy what you sell this morning. The assistant answered. The only question is whether the business it named was yours, and the answer to that is written on pages, or it is not.

## How to brief a video editor

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/how-to-brief-a-video-editor/ · Creator growth · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

One idea per beat, the hook, captions for the muted viewer, the cut process, the date, what a good brief contains and what a bad one does to the edit, written from the desk where we cut.

Most bad short videos were briefed badly, not cut badly. The editor received a folder of footage, a sentence that said make it pop, and a deadline that had already passed. What came back was exactly what was asked for, which is the problem. This is how to brief an editor so the first cut is close and the second is final. We cut in-house, so it is also the brief we write for ourselves.

**The short version.** Give the editor one idea per beat, a hook that lands in the first second, caption text written for a phone with the sound off, a publish date to cut backwards from, and a reference that is the same kind of video. Expect two rounds of notes, consolidated, not a stream. A brief that does those things gets a usable first cut. One that does not gets a guess.

### What is the one-idea-per-beat rule?

A beat is a few seconds of video that carries one thing: one object, one claim, one movement, one line. A short video is three or four beats. The rule is that each beat carries one idea and no beat carries two. If a beat has to say the product is handmade and that it ships tomorrow, it is two beats, or one beat about whichever matters more.

The rule exists because a viewer on a phone decides to stay or go several times inside a single video, and each decision is made on whichever idea is in front of them. Two ideas in one beat means neither lands, and the viewer leaves on the confusion. The editor cannot fix this in the cut. The brief has to arrive already split into beats, each one a line, in order.

Write them as a list. Beat one: the overcoat, close, in the case. Beat two: the name on the collar. Beat three: the winter he wore it through. Beat four: the museum's name. An editor who receives that list knows what every shot is for before opening the footage.

### What does the hook have to do?

Earn the second second. The first second of a short video is the whole audition; a viewer who is not held by it is already gone. So the hook is the single most interesting frame or line in the piece, and it goes first, before the logo, before the context, before anything that assumes the viewer has decided to watch.

The brief names the hook. Not something attention-grabbing, which asks the editor to guess what you find interesting, but the actual shot or line. Open on the hand turning the collar over to show the name. Open on the caption that says he wore this for the whole of that winter. If you cannot name the hook, you do not yet know what the video is about, and the editor is about to find that out the expensive way.

A logo is never the hook, nor a slow fade from black, nor a title card with the name of the series. Each tells the viewer the interesting part is later, and the viewer takes you at your word and leaves.

### Why write the captions for a muted viewer?

Because most people watching on a phone have the sound off, in a queue, in a lift, in a meeting they are pretending to attend. If the idea is only in the voice, it did not reach them. The caption carries the idea; the sound is for the people who turned it on.

This changes what the brief contains. The caption text is written in the brief, word for word, per beat, before the edit starts. Short lines, one per beat, in the order the beats land. The editor's job is to place them and time them, not to write them, because the person who knows what the video is about is the person briefing it. A video briefed without caption text comes back with a transcript of the voice, which is the wrong thing: a transcript is what someone said; a caption is what the viewer needs to know.

Write the captions, read them with the sound off in your head, and ask whether the video still makes sense. If it does, the brief is nearly finished.

### How does the cut process actually run?

The order we work in.

1. Selects. The editor pulls the usable shots against the beat list and sets aside the rest. Nothing is cut yet; this is sorting.
2. The assembly. Beats in order, roughly timed, no music, no captions. It is ugly on purpose. It exists to answer one question: does the footage cover the beats?
3. The first cut. Timed properly, the hook in place, captions placed from the brief, music if the brief asked for it. This is the cut you give notes on.
4. Notes, once. Everyone who has an opinion gives it in one document, in one round, in the order the video runs. The editor takes the document and makes the second cut.
5. The second cut. This should be the final. If it is not, the brief was wrong, not the editor, and the fix is in the brief.
6. Export, check, publish. The export is watched on a phone, once, with the sound off, before it goes anywhere.

The notes step is where most briefs fail: notes arrive as messages over three days from four people, and the editor cuts against a moving target. One document, one round, one person collecting it. That is the whole discipline.

### Why does the date matter so much?

Because the edit is cut backwards from it. A publish date tells the editor when selects must be done, when the first cut must be ready and when notes must be in, and it tells everyone else that late notes are late. A brief without a date is a wish, and a wish is cut whenever there is a gap.

Put the date in the first line of the brief. Then put the date the notes are due, which is earlier than people like. A video that misses its date because the notes arrived the night before is not an editing failure, and the editor will remember who made it one.

### What does a good brief contain?

One page. A brief that needs two pages is two videos.

| Line | What goes there | Why the editor needs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The one line | What the video is about, in a sentence a stranger would understand | Every cut decision is made against it |
| The audience and the place | Who watches, and on which feed | Sets the ratio, the length and how loud the hook must be |
| The hook | The exact opening shot or line | The first second cannot be guessed |
| The beats | Three or four, one idea each, in order | The spine of the edit |
| The captions | The words on screen, per beat, as they will appear | Written by the person who knows the subject |
| Sound | Voice, music, neither, and the track if there is one | Changes the pacing of every cut |
| The close | The last frame: a name, a question, a place to go | The end is the second most watched moment |
| The reference | One video of the same kind that does what you want | A reference of a different kind is a trap |
| The date | When it publishes, and when notes are due | The edit is cut backwards from it |
| The do-nots | Anything that must not appear: a logo first, a slow fade, a face without consent | Cheaper to say than to re-cut |

A good brief fits on a phone screen. Everything the editor would otherwise have to ask is already answered, which is the only reason a first cut can be close.

### What does a bad brief do?

It makes the editor the author, and the editor was not in the room. Four kinds come up over and over.

- The adjective brief. Make it pop, something fresh, more energy. None of those is a decision. The editor guesses, the guess is wrong, and the notes round becomes the brief that should have existed on day one.
- The everything brief. Everything the business does, in one video, because the footage was expensive. The result says nothing, because it says everything. Cut it into four videos with one idea each; the footage will go further.
- The late brief. Footage first, brief after. The editor makes selects against no beat list and half of them are useless. Write the brief before the shoot, so the shoot covers the beats.
- The wrong reference. A cinematic brand film sent as the reference for a product reel, or a comedian's cut sent for a museum's object series. The reference has to be the same kind of video, or it tells the editor to make a different thing.

Every one of those costs a round of notes, and a round of notes is a day. A bad brief does not save time at the start; it moves the time to the end, where it is more expensive and everyone is tired.

### How do we cut in-house?

Khizer cuts our short video, and he is in the brief meeting before anything is filmed. That is the arrangement we would recommend to any brand that films regularly: the editor reads the beat list before the shoot, so the selects are quick. The brief is the contract between the person who films and the person who cuts, and it is written once, by the person who knows the subject, with the caption text in it.

The editor is not the author and should not have to be. Give the editor the idea, split into beats, with the hook named, the captions written, the reference right and the date on the first line. Then the first cut is close, the second is final, and the video goes out on the day it was meant to. That is not a trick. It is a page, written before the camera comes out.

## What a website redesign costs

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/what-a-website-redesign-costs/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

The three things that set the price, what a redesign should be judged on, who keeps the code, and when the right answer is not to redesign at all. No figures, on purpose.

Nobody can tell you what a redesign costs before they know what the site has to do, and anyone who gives you a number on the first call is pricing your patience, not your site. What we can tell you is what moves the price, what the finished site should be judged on, and when the honest advice is to leave the thing alone. There are no figures in this piece. There would be no honest way to include one.

**The short version.** Three things set the price of a redesign: how many kinds of page there are, how many other systems the site has to talk to, and who writes the words. Judge the result on the checkout, the speed and whether it can be found, not on how it looks in a portfolio. Keep the code and the accounts in your name. If the current site sells, is fast and ranks, do not redesign it; fix the one page that leaks.

### What sets the price?

Pages, integrations and content. Everything else a studio puts on a quote is detail inside one of those three, and a quote that cannot be sorted into them is hiding something.

#### Pages, meaning kinds of page, not count

A site with a hundred product pages built from one template is a small job. A site with a dozen pages that are each their own layout is a large one. The price follows the number of distinct designs, because each one has to be designed, built, tested on a phone and made to hold up when the words are longer than the mock-up. Ask any studio to count templates, not pages, and watch the quote move.

#### Integrations, meaning what the site has to talk to

Payments, stock, shipping, a booking system, a newsletter list, an accounting package, a customer record. Each one is a conversation between your site and somebody else's system, and each one has to keep working when the other side changes its mind. This is where most quotes go wrong, because the buyer says it just needs to connect and the studio hears a week of work. Name every system on the first call, and say which direction the data flows.

#### Content, meaning who writes the words

A redesign where the client supplies finished copy, photographs and product descriptions is one price. A redesign where the studio has to write them is another, and usually the larger, because the words take longer than the layout and no template saves you. The question to ask yourself before the call is simple: does the text exist, and is it good? If the answer is no, the redesign is a content project with a website attached, and it should be priced as one.

### What should a redesign be judged on?

Three things, none of which is how it looks in a screenshot.

- The checkout, or whatever the site's equivalent is: the booking form, the enquiry, the call. Can a stranger get from the first page to the thing that makes you money without hesitation, on a phone, with one thumb? Count the steps before and after.
- The speed. A page that loads slowly on a phone on a weak connection loses the visitor before the design is seen. Speed is a design decision, made in the choice of image sizes, scripts and hosting, and it is the first thing we check on any site we are asked to replace.
- The search. Does the site come up for the words your customers type, and does an assistant quote it when asked about what you sell? A redesign that drops a ranking the old site had has cost you twice, and the second cost is the one nobody puts on the quote.

A studio that shows you its portfolio is showing you the first impression. Ask instead for a site it built that you can buy from, and buy something. The checkout tells you more about the studio than the home page ever will.

### What did building for the checkout look like?

Seyr is a storefront we built around the purchase rather than the portfolio shot. The brief was what a buyer needs to see, in the order they need to see it: the product, the detail, the price and the path to paying, with nothing in between that exists to impress another designer. The product images are sized to the frames they sit in. The scripts are the ones a checkout needs and no others. The client has run it since the handover, with the build documented, which is the other half of what a redesign should be judged on.

It was built to convert, not to win awards. That sentence was the brief, and every decision that followed, including the ones that made it less photogenic, came from it.

### What did the shop rebuild look like?

Frank Zoller Authentic History is a militaria auction house in the United States. We rebuilt zollerhistory.com and added a shop for the pieces it sells outside the auctions, so that a collector searching for the house lands on its own page rather than on an auction platform's, and finds something to buy when there is no auction running.

The three things above all applied. The kinds of page were few and filled many times over. The integrations were the auction platforms the house already sold through. And the content problem was solved before the site was, because the house already had its archive and the listing platform we built for it, which writes descriptions from photographs, so the pages had something to be filled with. A rebuild for a business with thousands of items is a template and a pipe, and the price is in getting both right rather than in the number of pages the pipe fills.

### Who keeps the code?

You do. The code, the domain, the hosting account, the payment account and every login are in your name from the first day, with our access granted by you and revocable by you. The build is documented so the next person, who may not be us, can read it. That is not generosity; it is the thing that makes the fee honest. A studio that holds your code holds your site hostage at the first disagreement, and a quote from a studio that will not put ownership in writing is not a quote you can compare to anyone else's.

Ask every studio the same question before the price: if we part ways in a year, what do I have? The answer should be a repository, a domain and a hosting account you can log into without them. Anything less is rent, and rent is the one cost of a redesign that never appears on the quote.

### When should you not redesign?

More often than a studio will tell you, because a studio is paid for the rebuild and not for the advice.

- When the current site sells. If people buy, book or call from it, the redesign risks the thing that works for the thing that looks newer. Fix the slowest page and leave the rest.
- When the problem is traffic, not the site. A site nobody visits does not need a new design; it needs search work, ads or content, and all three are cheaper than a rebuild and reversible.
- When the words are the problem. A site that says nothing clear will say nothing clear in a new layout. Rewrite first. Sometimes that is the whole job.
- When the checkout belongs to someone else. A store on a platform with its own checkout does not need a custom build to sell more; it needs the template tidied and the product pages written.
- When you cannot name the number. A redesign without a target, whether orders, enquiries, speed or a ranking, cannot be judged, and a project that cannot be judged cannot succeed.

If none of those is you, the redesign is worth pricing, and the price will come from the three things at the top of this page. Bring the list of systems, the state of the words and the number you want the site to hit. Then the quote is about the work, which is the only thing it should ever have been about.

## Why we publish our prices

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/why-we-publish-our-prices/ · How we work · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

What hiding the fee costs the buyer, what a published number does to the first call, the two fees and the tailored tier, why ad spend is never a percentage, and what we give up by saying it.

Our fees are on the pricing page, in dollars. Most agencies will not do that, and the reasons they give are sincere: every client is different, the scope sets the price, a number on a page would be misread. All true. All also convenient. This is the full case for publishing, including what it costs us, so you can judge whether the agency you are talking to has a reason or an excuse.

**The short version.** An agency that hides its fee is pricing you, not the work. A published fee turns the first call from a qualification into a conversation about your number. Ours are $2,000 a month for one channel and $4,000 a month for the full loop; larger work is priced to the result you want. Ad spend is yours, stays in your account, and we never take a share of it. Publishing costs us enquiries, and we publish anyway.

### Why do most agencies hide the fee?

Because a hidden fee can be set after the agency has looked at you. The discovery call is not for discovering your business; it is for discovering your budget. The questions sound like diligence. What is your revenue, what did you spend last year, who else are you talking to. Each one narrows the number the proposal will carry, and the proposal arrives a week later with the fee set to what you looked able to pay.

This is not villainy. It is how an agency with a mixed book of clients keeps its margin: the fee stretches to the client, and nobody on the client's side can compare it to anything. It depends is a true sentence. It is also the most profitable sentence in the industry, and it is said most often by the people who benefit from it most.

There is a second reason, less discussed. A hidden fee protects an agency from its competitors. If nobody publishes, nobody has to defend a number against a rival's number, and the comparison the buyer most wants to make is the one the buyer cannot make.

### What does that cost the buyer?

Time first. A hidden fee means a call to find out whether a conversation is even possible, then a proposal, then a week, then the discovery that the number was never within reach. Multiply that by the three or four agencies a careful buyer talks to and the search has eaten a month before a single ad has run.

Then the comparison. With no published number, the buyer compares proposals, and proposals are written to be incomparable: different scopes, different bundles, different words for the same work. The buyer ends up comparing decks, which is comparing the sales skill of the people who wrote them.

Then the anchor. A fee that arrives inside a proposal arrives beside a list of everything the agency will do, and it is read against that list rather than against the market. The buyer has no idea whether the number is high, because the only number they have seen is this one. A founder who cannot audit the work, and most cannot, has lost the one thing they could have audited: the price.

### What does publishing do to the first call?

It removes the qualification. Nobody books the call to find out whether they can afford us, because they already know. They book it to find out whether we can get them to the number they need, which is the only question worth thirty minutes of anyone's time.

So the call is thirty minutes, there is no deck, and it starts at your number rather than ours. You tell us what you need the business to do by the end of the quarter. We tell you, out loud, whether we think the work can get there and what it would take. If the answer is no, the call ends early and nobody has been pitched. Nobody who guarantees a number is telling you the truth, and a call that starts with the fee settled has no reason to pretend.

The published fee also loses the wrong enquiry before it costs anyone a call. The person who wanted the cheapest possible price leaves the pricing page without booking, which is the right outcome for both of us. The person who stays has already decided the fee is possible, so the call is about the work.

### What are the two fees?

Two published numbers and a third tier that is written to your target. The full list is on the pricing page; the shape is below.

| Tier | The fee | What it buys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starter | $2,000 a month | One channel, picked on the first call: Meta ads on one account, or short video and carousels, or search pages and a researched article. A written report and a call every month. |
| Standard | $4,000 a month | The full content and findability loop: short videos, carousels and posters, page optimisations and researched articles, answer-engine entries, the Business Profile kept current, email campaigns, a visibility report and consultation hours. |
| Tailored | Priced to the number | Paid media at scale across Meta and Google, a custom AI product scoped against how it earns, photography and production, and everything in Standard, written to the revenue target you give us. |

Starter is one of the three, not all three. We say that on the page because the most common disappointment with any agency is a scope that was assumed rather than read. Standard excludes paid media management, on-site shoots and website builds, and says so in the same breath. The exclusions are what make the inclusions believable.

Tailored has no published number, and from a distance that looks like the thing this whole article argues against. The difference is the method. The fee is set against the number you want to hit, after we have seen the account, and we show you how we arrived at it. A price with its working shown is not a hidden price. A price that appears at the end of a deck is.

### Why is ad spend never a percentage?

Because a share of spend pays an agency more for spending more, and the agency is the one setting your budgets. That is the wrong incentive to hand to the person with a hand on the dial. The industry norm is a percentage, and the norm has quietly made every budget recommendation in the industry suspect.

Our fee is flat. Your advertising spend is yours, it is billed by the platform to your own card, it stays in an account in your name, and we never route it through us. The only way we earn more is if you decide the work was worth more and buy more of it. The spend and the fee live in different places on purpose, so you can always see which is which.

### What do we lose by publishing?

Enquiries. A number on a page lets people leave without talking to us, and some of those people could have been talked into a fee they could stretch to. We do not get to find out. That is a real cost and we feel it in the inbox.

Price. Some buyers would have paid more than the published fee and would have been content to. A hidden price would have captured that. A published one gives it away, every time, to everyone.

Competitors. Every agency in Karachi and a fair few in New York can read our rate card and undercut it by a dollar. We have made their pitch easier to write.

And the figure dates. We changed it once already this year and we will change it again, which means a page we have to keep honest, and an article like this one that reads the number from the same place the pricing page does rather than typing it twice. A published price is a maintenance commitment. Most agencies would rather not make it.

### So why do it anyway?

Because the buyer who cannot audit the work can audit the price, and a studio that says the number on the fee is easier to believe when it says the number on the result. We publish The Gallery's return on its ad spend and the hours the listing platform took off Frank Zoller Authentic History's desk, and both of those claims would be worth less coming from a studio that would not tell you what it costs.

Because the call is better. A first call that starts at the buyer's number, with the fee already settled, is the most honest half hour in this business, and it is the one we want to have.

And because we are not the cheap option and we do not pretend to be. A hidden fee lets an agency be whichever option the buyer hopes it is. A published one makes us say what we are, in advance, to everyone. That is uncomfortable, and that is the point.

### When is a published fee the wrong signal?

When the scope is genuinely unknowable at the start: paid media across several markets, a product that has to be designed before it can be priced, a shoot with a crew. Those are Tailored, and we say so rather than squeezing them under a published number that would be wrong in both directions. And when a buyer wants the fee to be the whole conversation. If the only question is whether we are cheaper than the next shop, the answer is no, and the pricing page has saved us both a call.

Everyone else gets the number before they get the pitch. Then the call is about what the number has to buy, which is where it should have started all along.

## Marketing a small museum

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/marketing-a-small-museum/ · Creator growth · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

The whole plan for a museum with a collection, a calendar and a staff of a few: the films, the event campaign, the event page that has to rank, the weekly rhythm, and what to count.

A small museum has the hardest marketing brief there is and the best raw material. The brief is hard because the staff is a handful of people who also run the desk, the shop and the school visits, and the budget is whatever is left after the roof. The material is the best because every case holds a thing nobody else has. This is the plan we run for the Gettysburg Museum of History, in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, written so a museum anywhere can run it with or without us.

**The short version.** Film the collection, not the building. Run one event campaign a year with a countdown, an object series and a page the museum owns. Make that page the thing that ranks for the event, and keep the museum's listing exact. Post from the collection every week on a rhythm the staff can keep. Count at the door and at the desk, not in a dashboard.

### Who is a small museum actually marketing to?

Three people, and they want different things. The first lives within driving distance and has never been in; they need a reason, which is usually an event or a single object they did not know was there. The second visited once, years ago, and needs to be reminded the place has changed. The third is far away and will probably never come, but follows the subject, watches every film and tells the first two. Most museum marketing talks to a fourth person who does not exist: a general public that wants to hear about heritage in the abstract.

Write for the three. The object film serves all of them. The event campaign is for the first and the second. The weekly feed keeps the third, who is where a museum's reach comes from. The Gettysburg Museum of History keeps uniforms, equipment and letters from the people who carried them, and the person who follows that subject from another state is not a lost cause. They are the one who shares the film.

### Why do the films come from the collection?

Because the collection is the one thing a museum has that nobody can copy. A film about the building looks like every other museum's film about its building. A film about a single overcoat, with the name of the man who wore it and the winter he wore it through, looks like nothing else on the feed.

The method is short. Pick an object with a person attached. Write one line about it before anyone picks up a camera; if the line needs a second sentence, pick another object. Film it close, in its case, in its own light. Cut it upright for a phone, with the object in the first second and the line over it. Close on the museum's name. We have written the method in full elsewhere in this journal. The point here is where it sits in the plan: the films are the anchor, every other post points back at one of them, and the archive of them is what a visitor scrolls through at the desk before deciding to come in.

For the museum we started on the floor with the curator, picked the pieces with a name, a date or a place on them, and filmed in series. A series matters more than any single film. It gives people a reason to come back, and it gives the staff a format they can keep producing after we have gone.

### What does an event campaign look like?

A small museum has one or two moments a year when a room has to fill. For the Gettysburg Museum of History it is the anniversary weekend in October. The campaign we ran for it is the shape we would hand to any museum with a date on the calendar and a quiet feed behind it.

1. A countdown, one story a day, each over an archive photograph, so the date is in front of the audience every morning without a flyer in sight.
2. An object series through the feed, one piece at a time, drawn from the people the weekend is about.
3. An invitation film cut from the collection, saying what will happen, where and when, in the voice of the place rather than the voice of a poster.
4. A small paid plan, in the museum's own ad account, putting the invitation in front of people within driving distance who have never heard of the museum.
5. One practical post, and only one, that does the job of the flyer: the day, the venues, where to park, where to go first.
6. Every one of the above pointing at one page the museum owns.

Nothing in it was a poster with a date on. Every post showed something from the collection or the archive, and the practical information rode on the back of it. We publish no figures from the campaign, because none has been measured and cleared, and a museum's weekend is counted at the door in any case.

### Why host the event page yourself?

Because the people searching for the weekend should land on the museum, not on a listings site, a ticketing platform or somebody else's write-up of last year. A third-party page that ranks for your event holds the one asset that compounds, and it will be wrong about the time.

We built the event page on the museum's own site, wrote it around the words people actually type for the weekend, and sent every story, post and film to it. It does three jobs. Before the event it carries the programme, the date, the venues and the answer to every question the inbox would otherwise get. During the weekend it is the link in the bio. Afterwards it becomes the record, with the photographs, the thanks and the first mention of next year, and it keeps ranking long after the posts have scrolled away. Next year's campaign starts from a page that already ranks.

The same discipline applies to the museum's listing on Google and on Maps. Opening hours, the address, the pin and the photographs have to be exact and current, because the listing is the first thing a visitor sees and a wrong closing time undoes a month of good posts. Enter the event on the listing in the same words as the page, and both do better.

### What should a small museum post each week?

A museum does not need a campaign to have a feed. It needs a rhythm it can keep with the staff it has. The question is never what could be posted; it is what two people can make on a Tuesday afternoon between a school group and the shop. The week below is built around that.

| Day | The post | Who makes it, and how long it takes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday | One object, one line, filmed upright on a phone | The curator and whoever is on the desk, under an hour |
| Wednesday | A face from the archive with a name and a sentence | Anyone who can scan a photograph, a few minutes |
| Friday | Behind the glass: a drawer opened, a label written, a repair in progress | Whoever is doing the work that day, filmed by the person next to them |
| Weekend | A question the curator cannot answer, put to the audience | The curator, one sentence |
| When it happens | A visitor at a case, with permission, or the next event carried on an object | The desk |

On a quiet week, three of those is enough. The order matters less than the habit. What matters is that none of them requires anything the museum does not already own, and that the object post is never skipped, because it is the one the others point back to.

### What should a museum count?

Not likes. A small museum has three numbers that mean something and all three are counted in the building. The door: how many came in, against the same week last year. The desk: the answer to the question of how they heard about the place, asked of everyone and written down. The event page: whether it comes up when someone searches the event's name and the town, which the museum can check on its own phone in a minute.

We report what the feed did alongside those, but we would never ask a museum to judge the work on reach alone. Reach that does not turn into a person at a case is a pleasant chart. The desk question is the only attribution a small museum needs, and it costs nothing.

### When should a museum not hire an agency?

When the collection has not been photographed. The first job is a camera and a list, and that is staff work, not agency work. When there is nobody to answer the inbox, because a campaign that brings questions to an empty inbox does harm. When the event is weeks away and nothing exists yet, because the page needs time to rank and the countdown needs an archive to draw on. And when the budget would come out of conservation, because the object has to exist before it can be filmed.

If the collection is photographed, someone answers the messages and the next date is a season away, the plan above works, with us or without us. We would rather a museum run it alone than not run it at all. The collection was always the content. The plan is only the order in which to let it out.

## Selling on Instagram in Pakistan

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/selling-on-instagram-in-pakistan/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

The inbox is the checkout, cash on delivery is the payment, and the ad's only job is to start a conversation. The operator's version, with The Gallery's result.

Most advice about selling on Instagram was written for a market with a card in every wallet and a checkout on every site. Pakistan is not that market. Here the buyer sees the post, sends a message, asks the price, confirms a size, and pays the courier at the door. Treat that as a defect and you will spend a year fixing something that was never broken. Treat it as the funnel and it sells.

**The short version.** The sale closes in the DM, the payment is cash on delivery, and the ad exists to start the conversation, not to send traffic to a page. Reply within minutes with the price and the options, confirm before the courier does, add a store only when the inbox cannot hold the catalogue, and measure delivered orders, never likes. The Gallery ran exactly this and got $5.20–$6 back for every $1 of ads, on every campaign to July 2026.

### Why does the sale close in the inbox?

Because trust does. A buyer here wants to know that there is a person behind the page, that the product exists, that the price is the price, and that the thing will arrive. A message answers all four in a minute. A checkout page answers none of them, and asks for a card that many buyers do not have or do not want to use online.

The inbox also does the selling a page cannot. Personalised products need a conversation: a name, a spelling, a date, a colour. A buyer who was undecided on the post decides in the reply. Instagram knows this, which is why its advertising can be optimised toward messages rather than clicks, and why a campaign built for a Pakistani brand should be.

### What does cash on delivery do to your numbers?

It moves the risk to you. The order is not a sale until the courier has been paid, and a share of orders will be refused at the door, or never answered when the rider calls. That share is the number that decides whether the business works, and it is set by what happens in the inbox before dispatch, not by the ad.

Confirm every order before it ships: a message that repeats the product, the price, the address and the delivery window, and asks for a yes. Call the ones who do not reply. Ship nothing unconfirmed. The brands that lose money on cash on delivery are the ones that treat the first message as the order. The ones that make money treat the confirmation as the order and the first message as a lead.

### What does the reply script look like?

Speed first. A buyer who messaged you also messaged two other pages, and the first clear reply usually wins. Then the script, which is not a sales pitch but a short set of answers in the order the buyer needs them.

| The buyer says | You reply with | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “Price?” | The price, the sizes or options, and the delivery charge, in one message | Three questions answered before they are asked; nothing to wait for |
| “Is this available?” | Yes, the options in stock, and the delivery time to their city | Confirms the product exists and that you know your stock |
| A screenshot of a post | The product name, the price and the one question you need answered to proceed | Moves from browsing to ordering in a single step |
| “Can I get it by Friday?” | A true answer, and the alternative if the answer is no | A missed promise is a refused parcel |
| Nothing, after the price | One follow-up the next day, with nothing new to say except that you are here | Many inbox sales close on the second message, not the first |
| “Yes, order it” | The full order read back, with the address and the amount the courier will collect, and a request for a yes | This is the sale. Everything before it was a lead |

Write the script down and give it to whoever holds the phone. The inbox is a sales desk, and a sales desk that improvises loses orders to one that does not. Saved replies on the platform make the first message near-instant; a person takes over at the first question the saved reply cannot answer.

### When should you add a store?

Later than you think, and for a different reason than you think. A store does not replace the inbox here. Most buyers will still message. What a store does is hold the catalogue, so the inbox stops being asked what else you have, and it gives the brand a place that looks like a business to a buyer who has not yet decided whether to trust the page.

Add one when the inbox is answering the same catalogue question all day, when repeat buyers ask for a link, or when you start selling outside Pakistan to people who do pay by card. Keep it simple, keep the prices the same as the ones quoted in the inbox, and keep cash on delivery as the first payment option on it, because that is still how most of the orders will arrive. The piece on store choice is at /blog/shopify-store-or-custom-site, and the Shopify page is at /services/shopify-stores.

### What kind of ad starts a conversation?

Not the kind that says shop now. An ad that ends in a checkout is asking for a decision the buyer is not ready to make. An ad that ends in a message is asking for a question, and questions are cheap to ask. The creative has to earn the question.

- Show the product being made, personalised or packed. Process is proof that it exists and that a person is behind it.
- Put the price in the creative, or the starting price. A buyer who messages knowing the price is halfway to confirming; one who messages to ask it often leaves when told.
- Ask the one question the buyer would ask you: what name, which colour, which date. The reply is the message.
- Use the platform's message objective, so the campaign is optimised toward conversations rather than clicks, and report conversations, not link taps.
- Run a tight set of creatives, cut the losers weekly and rebuild the winners. More creative does not help if nobody is reading the inbox.

### What happened for The Gallery?

The Gallery sells personalised newborn wear in Pakistan. Every product needs a name, a spelling and often a date, so the checkout was always going to be a conversation, and a campaign that pushed traffic at a product page would have measured the wrong thing.

We built ten creatives, each made to start a conversation rather than close a cart, and optimised the campaigns toward messages. The sale was tracked where it happened, in the inbox, and reported weekly against what had been agreed. Every campaign to July 2026 returned $5.20–$6 back for every $1 spent on ads. Not an average across one good quarter; every campaign. The spend behind the figure is not published, which we would rather say plainly than round away. The case is at /work/gallery.

### What should you measure?

Orders delivered and paid, and what each one cost in advertising. Everything else is a step toward that or a distraction from it.

| Measure this | Not this | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conversations started per campaign | Likes, saves, reach | A like has never paid a courier |
| Confirmed orders, and the share of conversations that became one | Link clicks | This is where the inbox either works or does not |
| Parcels delivered and paid, and the share refused at the door | Orders placed | Cash on delivery means an order is a promise until the rider is paid |
| Advertising cost per delivered order | Cost per thousand views | The only cost that can be set against margin |
| Reply time, in minutes | Follower count | Speed decides who wins the buyer who messaged three pages |

Keep a sheet. One row per order: the campaign it came from, the day it was confirmed, the day it was delivered, whether it was paid. That sheet is the report; the platform's dashboard is an input to it. An agency that reports from the dashboard alone is reporting on advertising. You are running a shop.

If we run it, the ad account stays yours, the spend stays on your card, and the fee is flat rather than a share of the spend, so telling you to pause costs us nothing. The longer piece on why the funnel is shaped this way is at /blog/the-dm-first-funnel-selling-on-instagram-in-pakistan, and the Pakistan page is at /pakistan/meta-ads-agency-pakistan.

## Writing auction lots from photographs

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/writing-auction-lots-from-photographs/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

The build in public: how an auction house that typed 1,250 lots by hand before every sale now fills them from photographs, and what it took to trust the machine.

Frank Zoller Authentic History runs militaria auctions in the United States. Before every sale, somebody sat down with the photographs and typed: a title, a description, a starting price and an estimate, one lot at a time, to lot 1,250. The work was not difficult. It was long, it sat in front of every auction, and it was done by the people who knew the most about the objects, which is the wrong use of them.

**The short version.** Photographs go in, listing rows come out. The model reads the image, checks it against a reference set of 32,000 past items, writes the lot in the house's own voice, scores its own confidence, and flags only the uncertain ones for a person. The first live auction ran on 16 August 2026. The house counts 400+ hours saved; what we watch is how few lots a person now has to read.

### What did the work look like before?

A sale starts with a room of objects. Each is photographed, the photographs are edited and renumbered, and then the cataloguing begins: what is it, what should it be called, what is it worth and what is the range a bidder should see. For a repeat item (a cap badge the house has sold a dozen times) the answer exists in the house's own history, if somebody remembers to look. For a new one, somebody has to know.

Multiply by 1,250 and the shape of the problem is clear. It is not one hard task. It is one easy task done more times than a person can do it without the quality sliding, and all of it has to finish before any of it can be sold. Every auction waited for the typing.

### What goes in, and what comes out?

Photographs go in: the same ones the house already takes for the listing. What comes out is the auction platform's bulk-upload template, filled: title, description, starting price, estimate range, one row per lot, ready to upload without retyping. The handoff is deliberately boring. The house's existing automation then cross-posts to its other bidding sites exactly as it did before, so nothing downstream had to change.

Between the two sits the engine. It identifies the object from the image, decides whether the house has sold one like it before, and either pulls that history forward or describes the object from what it can see. The voice matters more than people expect. A listing is a sales document with a reputation attached, and a house that has described things one way for years cannot start sounding like a machine on the day it starts using one.

### What is the reference corpus for?

Before the engine wrote anything, 32,000 past items went into a hosted backend: titles, descriptions, estimates and what each one actually sold for. That set is the house's institutional memory, in a form it could not be used in while it lived in spreadsheets and old catalogues.

It does three jobs. It teaches the model what this house calls things, so the output sounds like the house. It lets a repeat item carry its own history, so a badge that has sold before is priced against what it fetched, not against a guess. And it turned up something nobody had been able to see while the records were scattered: realised prices had sat consistently below estimates across the whole set. The estimates had been drifting upward for years, invisibly. That was a finding about the business, not about the software, and it was worth the ingestion on its own.

### How does the review step work?

This is the part that made it usable, and it is not the writing. Every output carries a confidence score. Above the line, the lot passes straight through to the template. Below it, the lot is flagged and a person reads it. Nothing else reaches a person.

A tool that needs every answer checked has saved nobody anything, because the checking is the job it was meant to remove. A tool that knows which of its answers to distrust has. The cataloguer's day moves from reading all the lots to reading the hard ones: the unfamiliar object, the ambiguous photograph, the item whose history is thin. That is where their knowledge was always most valuable, and it is now the whole of what they spend it on.

- The model could not match the object to anything in the house's history and is describing it from the image alone.
- Two plausible identifications, with nothing in the photograph to choose between them.
- A price that falls outside the range the house's past sales would predict for an object of that kind.
- A photograph that is too dark, too cropped or too busy to describe honestly.

The threshold is a dial, and it was set by the house, not by us. Set it high and more lots get read, at the cost of time. Set it low and fewer do, at the cost of trust. The right setting is the one where the person reviewing stops finding errors in the lots that were not flagged, and that is found by looking, not by argument.

### What did it take to trust it?

Nobody trusts a cataloguer on their first day, and the machine got the same treatment.

1. It ran beside the old process first. A past sale, already typed by hand, was fed through as photographs, and the output was read against what the house had actually written and what the lots had actually fetched.
2. The house's own people read the flagged lots and the unflagged ones, until the unflagged ones stopped surprising them.
3. The voice was corrected lot by lot until a reader could not tell which rows the machine had written.
4. The threshold was moved, deliberately, in both directions, to see what came through and what was caught.
5. Then one live auction, on 16 August, with a person watching every stage and the old process ready to take over if it had to. It did not have to.

What made the trust possible was the shape of the thing, not its cleverness. The output is a spreadsheet the house already used. The upload is the one they already did. The review is a shorter version of the reading they already did. Nothing in the house's day was replaced by something unfamiliar. A long part of it was made short.

### What does 400+ hours actually mean?

It is the house's own count of the typing that no longer happens, and it is open-ended on purpose: the saving continues with every sale, and we do not attach a period to it because the house has not. We would rather publish a number with its limits than round it into a headline.

The figure we watch more closely is the share of lots a person now has to read, because that is what decides whether the tool is working. If the flags creep up, the model has met a run of objects it does not know and the corpus needs feeding. If they fall to nothing, the threshold is probably too loose and somebody should check a sample. A good number sits in the middle and moves slowly.

The build sits beside the rebuilt zollerhistory.com and its shop, for the same house. The listing engine is the one we show first, because it is the clearest example we have of what we mean by an AI app: a narrow tool, built against a task somebody did by hand before every sale, with a review step that lets a person trust it. The case is at /work/zoller, the service page is at /services/ai-apps, and the piece on what a tool like this costs is at /blog/what-a-custom-ai-app-costs.

## What email marketing should cost

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/what-email-marketing-should-cost/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

Flows versus campaigns, the platform's fee versus the agency's, two things to refuse outright, and where the two emails a month in our Standard tier fit.

Email is priced strangely because it is two different products sold under one word. There is the software that sends the mail, which charges by the size of your list, and there is the person who writes it, who charges by the month, the email or the hour. Most quotes blur the two, and the blur is where the money goes.

**The short version.** You pay twice for email: the platform, which scales with your list, and the writing, which should not. Flows are written once and run themselves; campaigns are written every month and are the real cost. Refuse any quote that includes a rented list or reports on opens. Our Standard tier at $4,000 a month includes two campaigns a month inside the full content loop. Email is not something we sell on its own.

### What is the difference between a flow and a campaign?

A flow is an email that sends itself when something happens: someone subscribes, someone leaves a cart, someone has not bought in a while. It is written once, set up once, and then works every day without anyone touching it. A campaign is an email sent to the whole list, or a segment of it, on a date somebody chose: the monthly note, the launch, the sale.

The cost structures are opposite. A flow is expensive to build and free to run, and most of its value arrives in the months after the invoice. A campaign is cheap to build and expensive to keep building, because the cost is a person's attention every month for as long as you want the list to stay warm. An agency that charges you monthly for flows that were finished in week three is charging rent on finished work.

| Question | Flow | Campaign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When does it send? | When a trigger fires: a sign-up, an abandoned cart | When somebody decides: a date on a calendar |
| How often is it written? | Once, then revised a few times a year | Every time it goes out |
| Where is the cost? | In the setup | In the ongoing attention |
| How do you judge it? | Orders it recovers or starts, per month | Revenue and clicks from each send |
| What should you pay for? | A build with an end, not a fee that runs forever | A monthly fee that covers the writing |

### What does the platform charge, and what does the agency charge?

The platform fee is the easy one. Every mainstream email tool prices by the number of people on your list, from nothing at the bottom to a few hundred dollars a month for a list in the tens of thousands, with the send volume as a second dial. It is paid to the platform, on your card, in your account. If an agency is paying it for you, ask why, because the account and the list should be yours on the day you part.

The agency fee is for the writing, the design, the setup of the flows, the segmentation and the reporting. It comes in three shapes: a flat monthly retainer, a per-email price, or a share of the revenue the emails produce. The share model sounds aligned and is the one to be most careful with, because the agency then has every reason to send more, discount harder and claim every order the platform can attribute, and the platform attributes generously.

Per-email pricing suits a brand that knows exactly how many it wants and can brief them. A retainer suits a brand that wants someone to own the calendar. Whichever you choose, the setup of the flows should be priced as a project with an end, not folded into the monthly forever.

### What should you refuse?

Two things, without discussion.

- A rented or purchased list. Anyone who offers to “add contacts” to your list is offering to get your domain marked as spam. The people did not ask to hear from you, the mail providers know it, and the damage lands on the emails your real customers wanted. A list is built from people who gave you an address. There is no shortcut that survives contact with a spam filter.
- Reporting that leads with the open rate. The major mail apps now fetch every message on the reader's behalf, before the reader has seen it, as a privacy measure, and the platform counts that as an open. The number drifts upward whatever you send. An agency that puts it at the top of the report is either unaware of this or hoping you are.

A third, softer refusal: a discount in every email. It trains the list to wait, and it means the agency is buying its own results with your margin. The welcome can carry an offer. The monthly should be worth opening without one.

### Which three emails do most of the work?

A welcome, an abandoned-checkout email and a monthly note. The first two are flows and run themselves once they are written. The third is the campaign you have to keep writing. Between them they do most of what email can do for a brand, and almost everything beyond them is refinement.

- The welcome goes the moment someone subscribes. It confirms the decision, says what to expect, and asks one thing. It is the most-opened email you will ever send, so it should be written slowly.
- The abandoned-checkout email goes within the hour, then once more a day later. Its one job is to bring the buyer back to the cart, ideally without a discount. Judge it on orders recovered.
- The monthly goes the same week every month and carries one story, one product and one ask. Judge it on revenue and clicks, never on opens.

The longer piece on the three, what each should say and how to judge it, is at /blog/email-marketing-the-three-emails-that-pay. This one is about the money.

### How does email fit in our Standard tier?

Email is part of the full loop rather than a channel we sell on its own. Standard, at $4,000 a month, includes two email campaigns a month beside the videos, the carousels, the page optimisations, the articles, the answer-engine entries and the monthly call. The welcome and the abandoned-checkout flows are written and set up in the first weeks and then left running. The two campaigns are the monthly and a second, shorter note, usually a launch or a single story.

Starter, at $2,000 a month, does not include email at all. It is one channel, chosen on the first call: ads, content or search. If email is the thing you need and nothing else, we are the wrong shape for you, and a good freelance email writer on a per-email price will serve you better than our list will. We would rather say that on the call than sell you a loop you only need a third of.

The platform fee is never inside our number. It is yours, on your card, in your account, as the ad spend is. The list is yours, the flows are yours, and if you leave with thirty days' notice everything keeps sending exactly as it did the day before.

### What does a fair quote look like?

- The platform named, its fee stated separately, and the account in your name.
- The flows priced as a build with an end date, and listed: welcome, abandoned checkout, and whatever else is proposed, with the reason for each.
- The campaigns priced per month, with the number of sends, who writes them and who approves them.
- The report defined before the first send: revenue from email, orders recovered, clicks. Opens may appear in it; they may not lead it.
- No list bought, rented or “enriched”, in writing.
- What happens when you leave: the list, the templates and the flows stay yours, and the agency's access ends.

Email is the only channel you own. Nobody can change the algorithm on your list, and nobody can raise the price of reaching it. That is exactly why it should cost less than the channels that can, and why a quote that makes it the expensive one is telling you something about the quote. The service page is at /services/email-marketing.

## How a small brand shows up in AI search

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/how-a-small-brand-shows-up-in-ai-search/ · How we work · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

The five things an answer engine needs before it will name a small business, in the order to do them, with this site as the worked example.

When someone asks an assistant for a good agency in Karachi, or a personalised newborn gift, or who can catalogue an auction from photographs, the assistant names somebody. The names it gives are not the biggest brands. They are the ones it is most certain about. A small brand can be that, and most are not, because certainty is built from dull work nobody did.

**The short version.** An answer engine names a brand when it can find one consistent description of it, a page that answers the question in the first paragraph, a plain summary file at llms.txt, and profiles that all agree. It does not reward roundups, adjectives or volume. Fix the entity first, then the pages, then the file, then the profiles, and give it no reason to doubt you.

### Why does an assistant name one brand and not another?

An engine builds a picture of your business from every place it can read: your site, your Google listing, your Instagram profile, a directory you forgot, a supplier's page that mentions you. From those it decides two things: what you are, and how sure it is. The second decides whether you get named. A brand described five different ways in five places is five weak guesses. A brand described one way everywhere is one confident fact, and confident facts are what an assistant repeats.

Size helps only because big brands are mentioned more. A small brand cannot buy mentions, but it controls every one of its own, and that is enough for most of the questions it wants to be the answer to. The question is rarely who the best agency in the world is. It is who does this, here, for a business like mine, and that question has a short list.

### What is the entity, and why fix it first?

The entity is the machine's idea of you: one name, one place, one line about what you do. Most small brands have never written that line down, so it has been written for them, differently, by whoever filled in each profile. The company is a studio on the site, an agency on Google, a consultancy on a directory, and the address on one of them is the old one.

Write the line once. Who you are, where you are, what you do, for whom. Ours is one sentence: Drifted Marketing is a growth agency in Karachi, founded 2026, doing ads, content and AI apps for brands in the United States, the Netherlands, Australia and Pakistan. Then use that sentence, unaltered, everywhere a machine might read it. Spell the name the same way, with the same punctuation. Use one office address, written one way.

- The footer and the about page of your own site.
- The summary file at llms.txt.
- The structured data inside the page code, which a machine reads before it reads the copy.
- Your Google Business Profile, with the category matching what the site says you are.
- Every social profile, including the ones you stopped posting to.
- Every directory that lists you, including the ones you did not ask to be on.

Check it once a quarter. When something changes (an address, a name, a founder), change it everywhere in the same week, because a machine that finds the old and the new side by side does not pick the newer one. It trusts both less.

### What does an answer-first page look like?

An engine does not read a page. It lifts a passage, and the passage it lifts is the one that answers the question on its own, without the paragraphs around it. Most pages build to the point over six paragraphs because that is how people were taught to write, and the engine, which is not a person, has stopped reading by paragraph six.

So put the answer under the heading, complete, and then the detail. Make the heading the question the reader typed. If the question is what you charge, the first sentence under it is the price. If the question is whether you work with a category, the first sentence is yes or no, with the client named by company. Then explain.

Every piece in this journal opens with a boxed short version, labelled the same way every time, so the extractable answer can be found by pattern rather than by reading. The headings are questions. The fees are read from one file into every page that quotes them, so no page can quote a price the pricing page has changed.

### What is the summary file at llms.txt?

A plain text file on your own domain, at the address llms.txt, that tells an assistant who you are, what you do, where you are, what it costs and which pages matter. It is the one document on the web where you decide exactly how a machine describes you. A fuller version, llms-full.txt, can carry the important pages themselves, so an assistant does not have to crawl for them.

Write it the way you would brief a new colleague who will be asked about you by strangers: the one line first, then the services, then the proof you can name, then the price, then the links. Keep the top short, because the top is what gets quoted. Say nothing in it that a page on the site does not also say. A summary file that drifts from the site is a contradiction, and contradictions lower the engine's confidence in both.

Ours is generated from the same content files that build the pages, so it cannot disagree with them. A small brand without a build pipeline can do the same by hand: write the file from the site, not from memory, and update it the same day the site changes.

### Why do profiles matter when nobody reads them?

Because machines do. The Instagram bio you wrote in a hurry, the Google listing a former intern set up, the directory page with the old phone number: each is a source, and each one that disagrees with the site is a vote against you. The fix is not to post more. It is to make every profile carry the line, the same name and the same address, and link to the site.

Google Business Profile is the one that matters most for a local question, because it is the source an engine trusts for where you are and whether you exist. Keep the hours true, answer the reviews, post to it now and then, and make the category match what the site says you are. A listing that says one thing while the site says another is the most common reason a real business is invisible to an assistant that would otherwise have named it.

### Why do “best agencies” lists earn citations for your competitors?

The instinct is to write the roundup: the ten best agencies in your city, with yourself placed third for modesty. For a while engines quoted those pages, because they were shaped like answers. They have since learned what a reader learned earlier. A roundup written by one of the entries is an advertisement, and it knows nothing first-hand about the other nine.

Worse, it works against you in a specific way. A list page names your competitors beside you, in your own words, on your own domain. An engine reading it learns that those companies exist, what they do, and that you consider them peers. It now has nine more entities to be confident about, and the page it cites for the question is still not yours, because a list is not a primary source for anything.

Engines now prefer the page with first-hand knowledge. If the question is what an agency charges, the page that gets quoted is the agency's own pricing page, with a figure on it. If the question is how a campaign worked, it is the case page from the company that ran it, with the number and its date. Write those pages. Concede something on them, because a page that never admits a case where it is the wrong choice does not read like an answer to a comparison question.

### What does this site do, as the worked example?

| What the engine wants | What this site does | What a small brand can do by hand |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One consistent entity | One line, read into the footer, the summary file and the structured data from one place | Write the line once; paste it, unchanged, into every profile |
| An answer it can lift | A boxed short version at the top of every journal piece, with headings shaped as questions | Put the answer in the first sentence under each heading |
| A summary it can trust | llms.txt and its full version, generated from the same content as the pages | Write the file from the site, and update it the day the site changes |
| Facts it can check | Clients named by company, with the work and, where cleared, the number and its date | Name the client, give the number, date it, or say there is none |
| No reason to doubt | A check before every build that fails on any uncleared figure | Read every number on the site once and delete the ones you cannot defend |

The last row is the one that matters. We built the gate because we made the mistakes it catches, more than once, before it existed: a figure that reached a page without being cleared, a client's result attached to the wrong case, a number that was true once and quietly stopped being. An engine that finds one of those does not forgive the rest of the page.

What none of this can do is make a weak offer quotable. If there is no fact, there is nothing to cite. It does not replace ordinary search, which still sends most of the visitors. And nobody can promise you a citation, because the engine decides and changes its mind. What a small brand can do is give it no reason to doubt you, which is most of the work and almost none of the cost. The longer piece on the mechanics is at /blog/how-to-get-your-brand-cited-by-ai-search, and the service page is at /services/ai-search.

## What a Google Ads agency costs

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/what-a-google-ads-agency-costs/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

The three ways agencies charge for Google search, what each one pays them to do, where the money hides inside the account, and when Google is the wrong channel entirely.

Google Ads is the channel with the most honest intent and the least honest pricing. The person typing “emergency plumber near me” wants a plumber now, which is the best signal advertising has ever had. The agency selling you the management of that signal will usually not tell you what it costs until you have had the call. We would rather write it down.

**The short version.** Agencies charge for Google Ads one of three ways: a share of what you spend, an hourly rate, or a flat monthly fee. Each pays the agency to do something different, and only one of them pays it to spend less. Ours is flat and published: $2,000 a month buys one channel on the Starter tier, and paid media across Google and Meta at scale is Tailored, priced to the number on the first call. Your spend stays in your own account and we never take a cut of it.

### How do agencies charge for Google Ads?

Three models, and most agencies use one of them or a blend. A share of spend, where the fee is a slice of what you pay Google each month and shrinks as a proportion only once the budget is large. An hourly rate, where you pay for the time of a named specialist and the invoice follows the work. A flat retainer, where the number is agreed up front and does not move with the budget.

| Model | What you pay for | What it pays the agency to do | Where it goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Share of spend | A slice of your monthly budget | Grow the budget. Every recommendation to spend more is a raise | Small accounts get a junior; large accounts overpay for the same work |
| Hourly | A named person's time | Do the work it can log, and log it | Maintenance billed as strategy; the clock runs while you wait for a reply |
| Flat retainer | A fixed scope, in writing | Hit the number, however much or little that takes | Scope drifts in the agency's favour unless it is written down |

Read the third column twice. The model is not an accounting choice. It is the instruction you give the agency about what to want.

### What does a share of spend pay the agency to do?

It pays them to spend. That is not a cynical reading; it is the arithmetic. If the fee is a slice of the budget, the only way the agency earns more is for you to pay Google more, and every piece of advice points gently that way. Add the Display network. Turn on Performance Max. Raise the daily cap. Each of those may be right, and each is also a raise.

The advice you will not get on this model is the advice that saves you money. Nobody on a share of spend tells you that your brand-name campaign is buying clicks you would have had for free, or that the account has found its ceiling and the next thousand dollars buys worse leads than the last. Those sentences are pay cuts for the person saying them.

At the small end it fails the other way. A slice of a modest budget does not pay for a senior person, so the account is opened by whoever is cheapest, or by nobody, and the agency's margin depends on you never noticing.

### What does an hourly rate pay the agency to do?

It pays them to log hours, which is a better incentive than it sounds and a worse one than it should be. Hourly is honest about the one thing a share of spend hides: there is a person, and the person has a rate. A senior specialist's rate is high, and that is the real cost of the attention you are buying, whoever is invoicing you for it.

The trouble is what counts as an hour. Checking the search terms report is maintenance. Rebuilding the campaign structure is strategy. Both are billed at the same rate, and only the second is what you hired the person for. Hourly also charges you for your own questions, because the reply to your email is on the clock. It suits a short, defined job (an audit, a rebuild, a handover) far better than it suits a relationship.

### What does a flat retainer pay the agency to do?

It pays them to get the result for the least effort, which is exactly the incentive you want as long as the result is written down. A flat fee is the only model under which the agency can say “stop spending on this” without it costing them anything, and that is the only condition under which the sentence can be trusted.

What it hides is scope. Because the number does not move, every protection the agency wants lives in the words around it. Two retainers at the same price can differ by whether anyone writes new ads, whether landing pages are in scope, whether tracking is set up or merely blamed. The fee is only comparable once the scope sits beside it.

### Where does the money hide inside a Google account?

The fee is the visible cost. The account has quieter ones, and a buyer who knows the list reads an agency's report in a different light.

- Your own name. A campaign on your brand's name returns beautifully, because those people were coming anyway. It is the easiest way to make a report look good and the hardest to notice. Ask for brand traffic reported on its own line.
- Default settings. A new campaign opts you into the search partner network, the Display network and broad match on your keywords. Each one spends; none of them was your decision.
- The search terms you never see. What people actually typed before they clicked is the most useful report in the account. If it is not in front of you every month, nobody is reading it.
- Conversions that are not sales. A tap on the phone number is not a call. A visit to the thank-you page is not an order. Ask what the account counts, and whether the number it counts is the one you pay rent with.
- The black box. Performance Max often works and tells you almost nothing about why. An agency that runs everything through it has handed its judgement to Google and is charging you for the handover.
- The landing page. If the page after the click is weak, the account is blamed, the budget is raised, and the page stays weak. Ask whose job the page is before you sign.
- Ownership. Some agencies open the account under their own manager login. Leave, and the history, the data and the learning leave with it. The account must be yours, with the agency as a user on it.

### What do we charge for Google Ads?

One flat fee, and it is on the pricing page. Starter is $2,000 a month for one channel; on the published list that channel is Meta ads on one account, with four new creatives a month and weekly optimisation. Google Ads management, on its own or beside Meta, sits in Tailored: priced to the number we agree on the first call, and flat once agreed. If you want Google alone on a modest budget, say so on the call and we will tell you whether a one-channel fee makes sense or whether you should run the account yourself for a while.

Ad spend is separate. It stays in your own Google account, on your own card, paid to Google directly. No share of it, no media commission, no rebate from the platform that we keep without telling you. The fee does not move because you had a good month, and it does not move because you had a bad one.

The reason is self-interested as much as moral. A flat fee is what lets us tell you to pause a campaign, cut the Display network or move budget into email without it costing us anything. On a share of spend that advice costs the agency money every time it is given, and advice that costs money is given less often.

> Nobody who guarantees a result is telling you the truth.

### When is Google the wrong channel?

More often than an agency selling Google will say. Search advertising only works when people are already searching, and that is a smaller set of businesses than it looks.

- Nobody types it. A new category, a product people do not know they want, a gift bought on impulse. Personalised newborn wear sells on discovery, in a feed, and closes in a conversation; a search campaign for it buys only the handful of people who had already decided.
- The order is too small for the click. If a sale earns you a few dollars and a click in your category costs about that, the arithmetic is settled before the campaign starts.
- The listing already does it. A local service with a well-kept Google Business Profile, real reviews and photographs often gets the map result for free. Pay for ads only once you can see what the free listing already brings in.
- The page cannot close. Search traffic is the warmest a site will ever get. If a warm visitor does not convert, the campaign is measuring the page, and the page is the job.
- The budget would be mostly fee. If our fee would be larger than your media, do not pay it. Learn the account yourself, or hire a freelancer by the hour for a rebuild, and come back when the spend justifies a retainer.

We have no cleared Google case to show you, and we would rather say so than borrow one. What we can show is the method: an account that is yours, search terms read every week, brand traffic reported on its own line, conversions that are orders, and a fee that does not grow when the budget does. The service page is at /services/google-ads, and the Meta version of this question is at /blog/what-a-meta-ads-agency-costs.

## Website speed, in plain English

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/website-speed-in-plain-english/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

Why a slow page wastes ad money, the four things that make a site slow, what fast feels like to a visitor, and what we do about it on every build.

Every brand we meet has been told its website is slow and almost none of them has been told what that means. The reports are written in developer language, the scores change every time you run them, and the agency that built the site says it is fine. Here is what speed is, in plain words, why it costs you money, and what to do about it.

**The short version.** A slow page is a paid click you did not get.
