The causes are nearly always the same four — images too big, too many scripts, a server too far away or too slow, and a layout that moves while it loads. Fast means the page is there when the thumb stops, the words come first and nothing jumps. Every build we ship has a size budget and a test that fails when the site gets heavier.

### Why does a slow page waste ad spend?

You pay for the click the moment it happens. The platform does not refund you if the visitor leaves before the page appears, and on a phone, on mobile data, a surprising share of them do. They tapped an ad that promised something, got a white screen, and went back to the feed. The ad looks like it failed. The page failed.

The waste compounds. The platform sees a click that did not become anything and charges you more for the next one. The search engine measures the same slowness and ranks the page lower, so the free traffic shrinks as well. And the visitors who waited arrive irritated, which is not the state you want a buyer in on the first screen.

It is the same bucket we describe in every ad account review: if the ads are doing their job and the page is not, more budget just buys more visits to a leaking bucket.

### What makes a site slow?

Four things, and the order below is roughly the order we find them in.

| The cause | How it feels | The fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Images too big | A blank frame, then the picture appears in bands | Size every image to the frame it sits in, in a modern format, and load the ones further down the page later |
| Too many scripts | The page is visible but nothing responds to a tap | Remove every tracker, chat widget and plug-in that does not earn its place; load the rest after the page |
| A slow or distant server | A long pause before anything at all appears | Serve the pages from a network near the visitor, cached, so the server is not asked twice for the same thing |
| A layout that moves | You go to tap and the button jumps | Reserve the space for images, adverts and fonts before they arrive, so nothing shifts |

Most slow sites have all four, and the first two account for most of the delay. A page builder with a dozen plug-ins and full-size photographs straight from the camera is the usual starting point, and it can be made quick without a rebuild. It is a day of work, not a project.

The scripts deserve a sentence of their own, because they are the cause owners least expect. Every tool ever added to the site — the chat bubble, the pop-up, the heat map, the tracking tags from three different agencies — left a script behind, and each one runs before the visitor can tap anything. Most sites we audit carry tags that nobody on the current team can account for. Removing them is free, and it is usually the single biggest gain on the page.

### What does fast feel like to a visitor?

Nobody measures speed with a stopwatch. They feel it.

- The page is there when the thumb stops. No white screen, no spinner, no logo pulsing while something loads.
- The words come first. A visitor can start reading before the pictures land, and the pictures land where the words said they would.
- Nothing jumps. The button you were about to tap is still there when your finger arrives.
- A tap does something straight away. The menu opens, the image enlarges, the form takes the letter.
- The second page is instant. Once a visitor is in, moving around the site should feel like turning a page, not loading one.

That is the whole standard. A site that does those five things on a mid-range phone on mobile data is fast, whatever a scoring tool says, and a site that fails them is slow, whatever the agency says.

### How do you check your own site?

Open it on your phone, on mobile data, not on the office wireless. Open an ad, tap it, and count in your head. Do it on the oldest phone in the building, because that is closer to your customers’ phone than yours is.

Then run the page through Google’s free PageSpeed tool and ignore the score. Read the list underneath it instead: it names the heavy images, the scripts that blocked the page and the things that moved. Most of what it lists maps onto the four causes above. If you have Search Console, open the Core Web Vitals report and look at whether the pages marked poor are growing or shrinking over the months. Growing means somebody keeps adding weight.

### What do we do on a build?

Speed is a decision made at the start, not a fix applied at the end, so every build we ship starts with a budget: a maximum weight for a page, enforced by a test that fails when a change goes over it. A site cannot quietly get heavier if the build refuses to ship when it does.

Seyr is an ecommerce storefront we built around the purchase rather than the portfolio shot. The product images are sized to the frames they sit in and served in modern formats. The scripts are the ones a checkout needs and nothing else — no chat widget, no tag that nobody can name the purpose of. The pages are served from near the visitor, and the client runs it without us.

zollerhistory.com is the site of a militaria auction house, with an archive of past lots that a collector will search through for an hour. An archive is the hardest kind of site to keep fast, because every page carries photographs and the pages run into the thousands. We serve them as static pages, built in advance rather than assembled on each visit, so the server has nothing to do but hand them over, and we load the images as the visitor scrolls to them rather than all at once.

On both, the fonts load once and the layout reserves its space, so nothing moves. None of that is clever. It is the four causes, decided against before the first page was designed.

### When is speed not the problem?

When the page is fast and still does not sell, the page is saying the wrong thing. A visitor who arrives from an ad promised one thing and finds another leaves at the same speed whether the page took a moment or a second. Speed is the floor: it is what makes the rest of the page possible to judge. It is not the reason anyone buys.

So fix it first, because it is cheap and it is measurable, and then stop talking about it and look at what the page actually says. If the headline does not repeat the promise in the ad, no amount of speed will hold the visitor long enough to find out what you meant.

## The object is the content

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/a-museums-social-media-the-object-is-the-content/ · Creator growth · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

How a museum collection becomes a feed — the short films we make for the Gettysburg Museum of History, the October campaign, why the event needs its own page, and what to post every week.

Most museums post the building, the opening hours and a flyer for the next event, and wonder why nobody outside the mailing list sees it. The feed is empty because the collection is not on it. Everything a museum needs to stop a thumb is already in the cases. The work is getting it out from behind the glass.

**The short version.** Objects beat adjectives. Film the piece, say who carried it and where, cut it upright, and let the fact do the work the caption used to do. Build an event campaign around a countdown and an object series, send every post to a page the museum owns, and post from the collection every week whether or not there is an event to sell.

### Why does the object beat the adjective?

The Gettysburg Museum of History keeps its collection on open display in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania: uniforms, equipment, letters and the stories of the men who carried them. When we started, the collection was on the floor and not on the feed. The posts described the museum. None of them showed a thing you could only see there.

A jacket with a name on it stops the scroll. A paragraph about heritage does not. The difference is that an object carries a person, a place and a moment without having to claim any of them, and a viewer who stops for the jacket stays for the sentence that explains it. So the short films we make start with the piece, not the room. We film the object in its case, write one line — who wore it, where, and why it sits behind this glass — and cut it for a phone held upright.

That is the whole method, and it holds for any collection. A pressed flower, a ledger, a tool with a worn handle: each is a story if someone says whose it was.

### How does a collection become a feed?

The order we work in, for the museum and for anyone with cases full of things.

1. Walk the floor with the curator and pick the pieces with a person attached. Not the rarest. The ones with a name, a date or a place on them.
2. Write one line per object before touching a camera. If the line needs a second sentence, pick a different object.
3. Film the piece, close, in its own light. The room is context for a wide shot at most. The object is the frame.
4. Cut upright and short. The first second shows the object; the line lands over it; the museum’s name closes it.
5. Caption with the fact, then the question. The fact is what the viewer learns; the question is what they answer in the comments.
6. Number the series. An object series that runs in order gives people a reason to come back, and gives the museum a format it can keep producing without us.

The archive does the rest. A museum with a thousand objects has a thousand posts, and the ones that work point at which ones to make next.

### What did the October campaign look like?

The museum’s anniversary weekend in October needed a room full of people, and a feed that had been quiet needed to carry it. We ran a thirty-day campaign in one look.

A countdown story every day, each one over an archive photograph, so the date was in front of the audience every morning. An object series through the feed, one piece at a time, drawn from the men the weekend was about. An invitation film, cut from the collection, that said what would happen and where. A small paid plan to put the invitation in front of people within driving distance who had never heard of the museum. And one event post that did the practical job: one day, two venues, here is where you go.

Nothing in it was a flyer. Every post showed something from the collection or from the archive, and the practical information rode on the back of it. We publish no figures for the campaign, because none has been measured and cleared, and a museum’s weekend is counted at the door in any case.

### Why does the event need its own page?

Because the people searching for the weekend should land on the museum, not on a ticketing site, a listings aggregator or somebody else’s write-up. We built the event page on the museum’s own site, wrote it around the words people actually type for the weekend, and pointed every story, post and film at it.

The page does three jobs. Before the event it holds the programme, the date, the venues and the answer to every question the inbox would otherwise get. During it, it is the link in the bio. After it, it becomes the record — the photographs, the thanks and the first mention of next year — and it keeps ranking for the search long after the posts have scrolled away. A museum that lets a third-party site hold the event gives away the one asset that compounds.

The same applies to the museum’s own listing on Google and to the Foundation’s site. Write them so the person searching lands on a page the museum controls, and keep them current, because a wrong opening time on a listing undoes a month of good posts.

### What should a museum post every week?

A museum does not need a campaign to have a feed. It needs a rhythm it can keep with the staff it has, drawn from the collection it already owns. The week below is the one we would hand to any small museum.

| The post | What | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The object | One piece, one line, filmed upright | The anchor. Every other post points back to this |
| The face | An archive photograph and a name | People follow people, even the long dead |
| Behind the glass | A conservator’s hands, a drawer opened, a label written | Shows the work, and earns the trust |
| The question | One thing the curator does not know, put to the audience | Comments bring the post back in front of people |
| The visitor | A family at a case, with permission | Proof that people come, and what they look at |
| The reminder | The next event, carried on an object | The flyer, but with a reason to stop |

Six kinds of post, not six posts a week — on a quiet week, three is enough. The point is that none of the six requires anything the museum does not already have in the building.

### What does not work?

- Stock footage of the period. It belongs to everyone, so it says nothing about you.
- Captions that are museum labels. The label is written for someone already standing in front of the case. The caption has to earn the stop first.
- The building. It is the one thing every visitor has already seen.
- Dates without people. The anniversary of an event means less than the overcoat someone wore through it.
- Posting only when there is something to sell. A feed that wakes up for tickets is a feed nobody has followed.

The collection was always the content. A museum that films its objects, names the people behind them and sends every viewer to a page it owns does not need to buy an audience. It has one in the cases, waiting to be let out.

## Hiring an agency in Pakistan: what protects you

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/hiring-an-agency-in-pakistan-the-questions-that-protect-you/ · How we work · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

Five questions that separate a good agency here from a bad one — who owns the ad account, where the money goes, the notice period, who you will talk to, and what a published fee tells you.

The agency market in Pakistan is good and uneven at the same time. There is real talent, a cost base that makes senior work affordable, and a growing number of shops that work for clients abroad. There are also arrangements that leave a client owning nothing after a year of paying. The questions that tell the two apart are the same whether you are buying from Lahore or from London, and none of them is rude to ask.

**The short version.** Ask who owns the ad account, where your advertising money goes, how long the notice period is, who you will actually talk to, and whether the fee is published. A good agency answers all five in writing without being asked twice. Our own terms are below as one example of what a clear answer looks like.

### Who owns the ad account?

The advertising account, the business page, the website, the domain and the tracking all belong in your name, in your own business manager, with the agency added as a partner. That is the single most important line in any agreement and the one most often missing.

The common arrangement here is the reverse: the agency runs your campaigns inside its own account, for a reason that sounds practical. Paying a platform in dollars from Pakistan is awkward, the agency already has a card that works, and it is simpler for everyone. It is simpler right up until you leave, when you discover that the account, the audiences it learned, the tracking data and every result it ever produced belong to someone else. You start again from nothing, and the next agency starts from nothing too.

Ask the question plainly: at the end of this contract, what do I log in to, and what do I keep? If the answer involves exporting a report rather than keeping an account, the price is higher than the fee.

### Where does the money go?

Two payments should never be mixed: the fee you pay the agency and the money you spend on ads. The spend goes to the platform, from your card or your business manager, and the agency never touches it. The fee is a flat figure for the work, agreed in advance.

Watch for the fee quoted as a share of spend. It is common, it sounds proportionate, and it rewards the agency for spending more rather than for selling more. Watch too for spend billed through the agency with a margin on top, which is a fee you cannot see. If an agency must run spend on its own card because of how you pay, insist on the platform’s own receipts, every month, with no rounding.

The same applies to anything bought on your behalf — stock photography, software, a freelancer’s time. Receipts, at cost, or in your own name.

### What is the notice period?

The length of the lock-in tells you how confident the agency is in its own work. A contract that holds you for a year says the agency expects you to want to leave before the year is out. Thirty days is enough for any honest shop to wind down a campaign, hand over the accounts and write the final report.

Read the exit clause before the scope. What happens to the creative, the audiences, the pages and the passwords on the last day? Who pays for the month of handover? Is there a fee for leaving? A long notice period with a penalty is not a sign of a serious agency. It is a sign of one that does not expect to be kept on merit.

### Who will you actually talk to?

The person who pitched you is often not the person who will run the work, and the gap between the two is where quality goes. Ask, before you sign, who writes the monthly report, who sets up the campaigns, who replies when something breaks at nine in the evening, and whether any of those names has changed since the first call.

Then ask what exists outside their heads. Where is your account documented? What would a replacement receive on their first morning? An agency that can show you a redacted handover document from another client has thought about turnover. One that says it never happens has not.

### What does a published fee tell you?

A fee on the website tells you two things. The agency has decided what its work is worth, and it is willing to lose the enquiries for which that is the wrong number. Both are good signs. A price that is only available after a discovery call is a price that will be set by what the agency thinks you can pay.

Our own terms, as one example of what a published answer looks like. Starter is $2,000 a month for one of ads, content or search, picked on the first call and not all three. Standard is $4,000 a month for the whole content and findability loop. Tailored is priced to the number you give us. Advertising spend is separate, stays in your own account and is never a percentage of anything. Notice is thirty days. The accounts, the pages and the creative are yours, and the first call is thirty minutes with no deck.

We are not the cheap option and we do not pretend to be. There is always someone cheaper, and the questions above are how you find out what the cheaper price leaves out.

| The question | A good answer | A bad answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who owns the ad account? | You. We are added as a partner. | We run it in our account; it is simpler. |
| Where does the spend go? | To the platform, from your card, receipts monthly. | Pay us and we handle it. |
| What is the notice period? | Thirty days, no exit fee, handover included. | Twelve months, with a penalty for leaving early. |
| Who will I talk to? | A named person who does the work and writes the report. | Your account manager will be assigned after signing. |
| What does it cost? | A published fee, the same for everyone. | It depends. Let us set up a call. |

### What is different if you are buying from abroad?

Nothing about the five questions, and a little about the consequences. A dispute across two legal systems is not going to court, because pursuing it costs more than the amount in question. So the protection is structural rather than legal: hold every asset in your own accounts, keep the spend on your own card, pay monthly rather than in advance, and keep the notice short. Do all four and the worst outcome of a bad hire is one wasted month.

Ask for the overlap hours in writing, in your time zone, and test them during the pitch by sending a message at the edge of the stated window. Ask who reviews the copy and whether they are from your market. Pay for a small test before you commit to a retainer. These are the same tests you would run on an agency in your own city. The geography only changes how expensive it is to skip them.

A buyer who asks these five questions will lose a few agencies in the first conversation. That is the point. The ones that remain have nothing to hide about the account, the money, the exit, the people or the price — and those are the only ones worth a second call.

## The DM-first funnel: selling on Instagram in Pakistan

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/the-dm-first-funnel-selling-on-instagram-in-pakistan/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

Why the sale closes in the inbox here, what cash on delivery does to your numbers, the reply script that holds the order, and what to measure instead of likes.

In most markets an ad sends a buyer to a checkout. In Pakistan it sends them to your inbox, and that is not a problem to be fixed. It is the funnel. A brand that builds its campaigns, its creative and its reporting around that fact sells; a brand that keeps pushing traffic at a product page measures a broken account and a healthy business and cannot tell which is which.

**The short version.** Here the sale is a conversation. Build creative that earns a message, optimise campaigns toward the inbox, reply within minutes with the price and the options, confirm the order before the courier does, and measure conversations and delivered orders rather than likes. The Gallery ran exactly this and got $5.20–$6 back for every $1 of ad spend on every campaign to July 2026.

### Why does the sale close in DMs here?

Three reasons, and none of them is going away soon.

The first is trust. A buyer who has never heard of you will not type a card number into a page, and many do not have a card they would use online at all. They will, however, send a message, because a message costs nothing and a reply tells them whether a person is on the other side.

The second is the product. A great deal of what sells on Instagram here is made to order or chosen with help — a name on a blanket, a size that depends on a photograph, a colour that depends on the room. The question is not friction before the sale. The question is the sale.

The third is habit. People already buy from people on WhatsApp. An Instagram inbox is the same gesture with a shop attached, and asking a buyer to leave it for a checkout is asking them to change how they shop in order to buy from you. Most will not.

There is a fourth reason that is really a consequence of the first three. The brands that sell well here have made the inbox their shop window. The pinned stories, the highlights, the saved replies, the price list in the bio — all of it is built to answer the question before it is asked, so the conversation starts closer to the sale than a cold click ever would.

### What does cash on delivery do to your numbers?

It splits every order into three: placed, confirmed and delivered. An order placed in a message is a wish. An order confirmed by a reply, with an address and a phone number, is an intention. An order delivered and paid for at the door is revenue. Only the last one counts, and the gap between the first and the last is where most of the money leaks.

The leaks are predictable. The buyer changes their mind by the time the rider calls. The address was incomplete. The phone was off. The courier tried once. Each of those is a cost — the outbound delivery, the return, the packaging, the day of a product that could have sold to someone else — and none of them appears in the ad platform.

So the funnel has to carry the order through all three stages, not just the first. A confirmation message before dispatch, a delivery window the buyer agreed to, and a phone number checked by a call rather than assumed from the profile. The brands that do this see a delivered rate that makes the ads pay. The brands that skip it watch good campaigns lose money at the door.

### What does the reply script look like?

The inbox is where the campaign succeeds or fails, and most brands staff it as an afterthought. The script below is the one we hand to a client’s team on day one. It is short because the buyer is impatient and the person replying is busy.

1. Reply fast. Minutes, not hours. The buyer messaged three shops and will buy from the one that answered first.
2. Answer the question they asked before anything else. If they asked the price, the first line is the price.
3. Offer choices, not questions. Two sizes with prices beats asking what size they want.
4. Ask for the three things you need in one message: name, full address with a landmark, and the number the rider should call.
5. Send one confirmation message that repeats the item, the price, the delivery charge and the window. A buyer who has read it back is far less likely to refuse at the door.
6. Follow up once on silence, the next day, with something useful — a photograph of the piece, not a nudge.
7. Keep it human. A real name, a real tone, no scripted greeting. The reason they messaged instead of clicking is that they wanted a person.

Write the script down, keep it to one page, and hand it to whoever covers the inbox on a Sunday evening. The rules are the same whether the person replying is the founder or a cousin.

### What happened for The Gallery?

The Gallery sells personalised newborn wear in Pakistan. Every order needs a conversation — the spelling of a name, a date, sometimes a photograph of the nursery — so the checkout was already the inbox before we arrived. The question was whether paid ads could feed it without breaking it.

We built ten creatives, each one made to start a conversation rather than close a cart, and optimised the campaigns toward messages rather than clicks. The sale was tracked where it actually happened, in the inbox, and reported weekly against what had been agreed. Every campaign to July 2026 returned $5.20–$6 back for every $1 spent on ads. Not an average across one good quarter — every campaign. The spend behind that figure is not published, which we would rather say plainly than round away.

Nothing about that result came from clever targeting. It came from creative that asked for a message, a team that replied quickly, and a report that counted conversations and deliveries instead of reach.

### What should you measure instead of likes?

The ad platform will show you reach, engagement and a cost per click, and none of them tell you whether an order left the building. Build your own sheet with the numbers below and read it every week.

| The vanity number | What it hides | Measure this instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Likes and comments | Whether anyone wanted to buy | Conversations started, per creative |
| Reach | Who messaged | The share of conversations answered within the hour |
| Link clicks | A page nobody buys on | Orders confirmed with an address and a phone number |
| Cost per click | What a delivered order cost | Ad spend divided by delivered orders |
| Follower count | Repeat buyers | Buyers who ordered twice |

The last row is the one that decides whether the business is a business. A brand whose buyers come back can spend more to win them. A brand whose buyers never return is renting its customers from the platform one at a time.

### When is DM-first the wrong funnel?

When the product needs no conversation and the ticket is small, a checkout wins, and forcing those buyers through an inbox costs you the ones who wanted to pay and leave. When the catalogue is large, an inbox cannot show it. And when nobody can staff the inbox — if the fastest reply on a weekday afternoon is tomorrow morning — paid traffic into it is paid traffic wasted, and the first fix is a person, not a campaign.

Everything else sells in the inbox here, and most of it sells better there than it would on a page. Build for the door the buyer actually walks through.

## Read your own Search Console in ten minutes

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/read-your-own-search-console-in-ten-minutes/ · How we work · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

Google’s free report tells you exactly how people find your site. Three screens are worth your time and the rest is noise — what a drop means, what to fix first, and when to ask for help.

Google gives every site owner a free report on how its pages are found, and most owners have never opened it. The ones who have usually started at the top of the first screen, which is where the platform puts the numbers that feel good and mean the least. Here is the order we use when we open a client’s account for the first time. It takes about ten minutes.

**The short version.** Three reports matter: Performance, which tells you what people searched and which pages they landed on; Pages, which tells you what Google can and cannot see; and Core Web Vitals, which tells you whether the site is fast enough to be trusted. Read them in that order. A drop almost always has a boring cause before it has an interesting one.

### Which three reports matter?

Search Console has a long left-hand menu and most of it is for developers. For an owner, three screens carry nearly everything worth knowing.

| Report | The question it answers | What to look at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Performance | What do people type, and where do they land? | Queries and pages, sorted by impressions, over the last few months |
| Pages | What can Google see, and what has it dropped? | The list of pages marked not indexed, and the reasons given |
| Core Web Vitals | Is the site fast and stable enough on a phone? | Which pages are marked poor, and whether that list is growing |

Performance is the one you will spend most of your ten minutes in. Switch it to show pages rather than queries, sort by impressions, and read the top of the list. That is what your site is actually known for, which is often not what you thought it was known for. Then switch to queries and read the words people typed. Those are the words your pages should be using.

The Pages report looks technical and is not. It is a list of every address Google has met on your site and a verdict on each: indexed, or not, with a reason. Read the reasons rather than the counts. A page marked not found was deleted or moved; a page marked redirected has been replaced; a page marked crawled but not indexed was read and judged not worth keeping, which is a note about quality rather than an error. Core Web Vitals is simpler still. It groups your pages into good, needs improvement and poor, as measured on real visitors’ phones, and the only thing worth tracking is whether the poor group is growing.

### What does a drop usually mean?

A drop in clicks is the reason most people open the report, and the instinct is to assume Google changed its mind about you. Occasionally that is true. Far more often the cause is something somebody did to the site, and the date of the drop points straight at it.

1. A page was removed, renamed or redirected. Check the Pages report for anything newly marked not found. This is the most common cause and the easiest to miss.
2. The site was rebuilt or the template changed. New themes drop headings, strip descriptions and change page addresses without anyone meaning to.
3. A tracking change. If the property was reconfigured or the domain moved, you may be comparing two different things.
4. The season. Compare the same weeks last year before you compare the last four weeks with the four before them.
5. A competitor published something better for the query. Search the term yourself, in a private window, and look at who is above you.
6. A Google update. Real, and the last thing to blame, because there is nothing to do about it except make the pages better.

Work down the list in that order. If you reach the bottom without finding the cause, the drop is probably a ranking change and the fix is editorial rather than technical.

### Which pages do you fix first?

Not the home page, and not the page you like most. The pages worth an afternoon are the ones where a small change moves a real number.

- Pages with many impressions and few clicks. People see the result and do not choose it. The title and description are the fix, and it is an hour’s work.
- Pages sitting just off the first page of results. They are close. A better heading, a clearer answer and a link from a stronger page can carry them over.
- Pages that lost clicks recently. Open the page, then open the archived version, and look for what changed.
- Pages Google refuses to index, when they are pages you care about. The reason is usually stated plainly in the Pages report and usually fixable.

Leave alone the pages that already rank first for their query. Edits there are more likely to cost you than to help, and the time is better spent one rung down.

Keep a dated note of every change you make. When the number moves a few weeks later you will want to know which edit moved it, and the report will not tell you.

### What should you ignore?

Average position across the whole site. It blends a page that ranks first for its own name with a page that ranks somewhere far down for a term you never targeted, and the result means nothing. Look at position per query, for queries you actually want.

Total impressions. They rise when Google shows your page for more searches, which includes searches you have no business appearing in. Clicks are the number; impressions are the context.

The long tail of enhancement warnings. Breadcrumbs, sitelinks, structured data notices. They are worth a developer’s hour at some point, and they are almost never the reason a page is not being found.

### When should you call someone?

Most of what the report shows you can act on yourself, and the pages we fix first for clients are the same pages the list above would have sent you to. Some situations are not do-it-yourself.

- A manual action notice. Google has flagged the site for something it considers a violation, and the fix needs to be exact.
- A site move or a rebuild coming up. The damage from a bad migration is done on the day, and it is far cheaper to prevent than to repair.
- The Pages report shows a large share of the site marked not indexed and you do not know why.
- The Core Web Vitals report has gone from mostly good to mostly poor and nothing on the page changed. Something underneath it did.
- You have fixed the obvious things and the number has not moved for a season.

Whoever you call, open the report with them on the first call and ask them to read it back to you in plain words. If they cannot say what the top queries are and which pages carry them, they have not looked.

### The ten-minute version

1. Performance, pages tab, sorted by impressions. Read the top. That is what you are known for.
2. Performance, queries tab. Read the words. Those are the words your pages should use.
3. Compare the last few months with the same months last year, not with the months before.
4. Pages report. Anything newly not indexed that you care about is your first fix.
5. Core Web Vitals. If the poor list is growing, the site is getting heavier.
6. Pick one page with high impressions and low clicks. Rewrite its title and description today.

Do that once a month and you will know more about how your site is found than most of the people selling you search services. The report is free. The ten minutes is the only cost.

## An AI app that pays its rent

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/what-an-ai-app-for-a-small-business-looks-like/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

Not a chatbot on the website. One narrow tool that removes one long job — what that looks like in practice, what it costs to own, and when buying beats building.

Ask a small-business owner what an AI app would do for them and most will describe a chatbot. Ask us and we will describe a job. The tools we build for clients do not talk to customers. They take one long, repetitive piece of work off a desk, do it well enough to be trusted, and leave a person to check the part that matters.

**The short version.** An AI app for a small business is a narrow tool that does one job you already pay for in hours. It earns its place by the time it removes, not by how clever it looks. Decide how it pays before anyone writes code, keep the scope to one input and one output, and make sure the code and the data are yours when it is finished.

### What does a working one look like?

Frank Zoller Authentic History runs militaria auctions in the United States. Every auction meant 1,250 lots entered by hand: photograph the item, then type a title, a description, a starting price and an estimate, one lot at a time, before a single piece could be sold. The work was not difficult. It was long, and it sat in front of every auction.

The platform we built takes the photographs and writes the listing rows. Behind it sits a reference corpus of 32,000 past items — titles, descriptions, estimates and the prices they actually fetched — so a repeat item pulls its own history and a new item is identified and described from the image. The filled template uploads to the auction site exactly as it always did. The first live auction ran on it on 16 August 2026, and the client counts 400+ hours saved.

The part that made it usable is not the writing. It is the review step. Every output carries a confidence score, and only the uncertain items are flagged for a person. Everything else passes straight through. A tool that needs every answer checked has saved nobody anything; a tool that knows which of its answers to distrust has.

There was a second finding we did not go looking for. Once the whole history sat in one place, it was plain that realised prices had been landing below estimates for years. Nobody could have seen that across a few thousand loose spreadsheets. That is the other thing a narrow tool does: it puts your own data where you can finally read it.

### Why is it so narrow?

Oorlogsspullen is a militaria shop in the Netherlands. The tool we built for it does one thing: it drafts a product listing from what the shop gives it, in the shop’s own voice, and a person reads the draft before it goes live. There is no dashboard, no account system, no settings page — nothing that was not needed to get a listing from a photograph to a draft. We publish no figures for it, because none have been measured and cleared, and we would rather say that than invent one.

It is narrow on purpose. Most of the value in a tool like this sits in one task, and most of the cost sits in everything built around that task to make it feel like a product. Every extra feature is a thing that can break, a thing somebody has to maintain, and a thing that makes the honest question — did this remove hours — harder to answer.

- One input, one output. A photograph in, a listing out. Nothing in between that needs a manual.
- No accounts. The moment strangers log in, you have acquired password resets, permissions and a duty of care.
- A visible review step, sized to how expensive a mistake is.
- Your own data as the reference, because that is the part no product on the shelf can copy.
- Documented well enough that the next person could run it without calling us.

### How do you know it pays its rent?

Before we build anything we ask the client one question: what does this replace, in hours or in money? If the answer is vague, the tool will be vague, and it will end up as a demo that impresses visitors and changes nothing. If the answer is specific — this many lots, this many hours, this person, every week — the scope writes itself and so does the test for whether it worked.

| Ask | A weak answer | A strong answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What does it replace? | It will help the team be more productive | The listing typing before every auction |
| Who does that job today? | Everyone, a bit | One person, most of a working week |
| How would you know it worked? | People will like it | The hours before the auction drop, and we count them |
| What happens when it is wrong? | It should not be wrong | A person reviews the flagged items |
| Who owns it in a year? | You, presumably | We do, with the repository and the documentation |

Measure for a month before adding a single feature. If the hours did not move, stop. You have learned something cheaply, which was the point of starting small.

### Should you build or buy?

Buy, most of the time. If software already exists that does most of the job, the part you compromise on is almost always cheaper than the maintenance you avoid. We say that against our own interest, because a build you regret costs us the relationship.

Build when the process is genuinely yours. The auction platform cleared that bar because the reference set was the client’s own history, and no product on the market has that history. The listing writer cleared it because the shop’s voice and categories are its own. If the reason your tool would work is knowledge nobody else has, it is worth building. If the reason is that you would like a tool, it is not.

### Who owns the code?

You do, and it should be written down before the first invoice. Ask for the repository in your name, with the agency added as a contributor rather than the other way round. Ask for the hosting in your own account, paid on your own card. Ask for the reference data to live somewhere you can export from. Ask for the documentation — the plain-language file that says what the tool does, how to run it and what to do when it fails.

Then ask the question that separates a build from a dependency: if we stopped working together on Friday, what would stop working on Monday? A good answer is nothing — you would need to find someone to maintain it, as you would with any software. A bad answer is anything that mentions a licence, a key or an account the agency controls.

### What does it cost to keep?

The build is the part on the proposal. The running costs arrive afterwards, and they are where budgets quietly break. The model behind the tool is billed on use, so real volume matters more than the demo suggested. The provider will change and reprice that model on its own schedule, and something that worked will stop working with no error message to tell you. And the review step is real work, done by a real person, every week — count it as a cost from day one rather than discovering it in month three.

A tool with nobody responsible for it does not break. It degrades, which is worse, because nobody notices until the output has been wrong for a while. Agree a monthly amount for care, or agree that there is none and mean it.

So the shape of the thing is unglamorous. One job. One input, one output. A review step sized to the cost of a mistake. Your own data, your own code, your own hosting. A number you measured before the build and again a month after it. That is what an AI app for a small business looks like when it is built to earn its keep, and it looks nothing like a chatbot.

## Shopify store or custom site?

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/shopify-store-or-custom-site/ · AI product · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

How to decide, why the checkout matters more than the award, when a custom build pays, what speed costs, and who keeps the code when it is done.

Almost every brand that asks us this question should be on Shopify, and we say so on the call even though a custom build is the larger invoice. The exceptions are real and they are specific. This is how to tell which one you are.

**The short version.** If you sell physical products through a normal cart, use Shopify and spend the difference on the product photography and the ads. Build custom when the site is part of the operation rather than a brochure: a catalogue the platform cannot model, a process the business runs through the site, or a checkout the platform cannot do. Either way, you keep the code, the theme and the accounts.

### How do you decide?

Ask what the site has to do that a standard store cannot. If the answer is nothing, the decision is made. Shopify's checkout is better tested than anything we could build you, its payment handling is a solved problem, and the thousand small things a store needs, taxes, shipping rules, returns, abandoned-cart email, are switches rather than projects.

1. You sell physical products with fixed prices through a cart. Shopify, with a good theme and no more than a handful of apps.
2. Your product is sold by conversation, a personalised item or a quote, and the checkout is the inbox. Then the question is the wrong one: you need a page that starts the message and a store that takes the money afterward, and Shopify does the second part fine.
3. Your catalogue is one-off items that change every week, each with its own history, estimate and provenance, feeding a sale process the platform has no concept of. That is an auction house, a gallery, a dealer. Build custom.
4. The site is where the work happens: staff log in, records are processed, something is generated. That is software with a shop attached, not a shop. Build custom, and scope the software before the shop.

If you are not sure which you are, you are the first kind.

### Why the checkout, not the award?

Most storefronts are designed for the portfolio shot: the full-screen video, the typographic flourish, the product hidden two scrolls down. They win design awards and lose sales, because the person who arrived from an ad wanted to see the product, the price and the shipping cost, in that order, on a phone, before the page finished loading.

Seyr is the storefront we built around the purchase rather than the shot. What a buyer needs to see, in the order they need to see it: the product, the detail, the price, the path to the checkout, with nothing between them that exists to impress another designer. It is the one place on this site where a visitor can click through to a finished thing instead of reading about it, and it was built to convert, not to win awards.

That is the standard for a Shopify build as much as for a custom one. The platform does not decide whether a store sells. The order of what the buyer sees does, and that is a design decision somebody has to make on purpose.

### When does a custom build pay?

When the site is part of the operation. Frank Zoller Authentic History is a militaria auction house whose catalogue is made of one-off items, each with a description, an estimate and a history, and whose listings are written by an AI platform we built from the photographs of each lot. zollerhistory.com and its shop are custom because the shop is the end of that pipeline, not a separate thing with a cart on it. A record is photographed, described, estimated and listed, and the website is where that record is seen. No store platform models an accession card.

A custom build pays when it removes work that happens every week, or when it makes a sale possible that the platform could not. It does not pay when its justification is that the brand is special. Every brand is special; most of them sell a product with a price through a cart, and a custom cart is a worse cart that costs more to keep working.

We decide how a build makes money before we build it. If the answer is a feeling rather than a number, the recommendation is Shopify, and we have made it to clients who came in wanting the larger project.

### What does speed actually cost?

A slow store spends its ad budget on visitors who leave before the page has said anything. Google measures how a page feels to use on real visitors' phones: how quickly the main content appears, how soon the page responds to a tap, whether things jump around while it loads. Those measures affect both where the store ranks and whether the person who arrived stays.

Shopify stores get slow in a predictable way: the theme was fast on the day it was installed, and then forty apps were added, each loading its own script on every page, until the product image arrives after the visitor has gone. The fix is a theme that does what you need without the apps, and an audit every quarter to remove what nobody uses.

Custom sites get slow in a different way: they were fast when they launched and nobody kept them fast. A custom build is only fast if someone owns its speed after the invoice is paid, which is a question to ask before you commission one. Whichever you choose, we measure the store on a phone over an ordinary connection before and after any change, and the measurement is in the report.

### Who keeps the code?

You do. The repository is in your name from the first commit, the theme lives in your store, the hosting is on your card, and the domain was always yours. We work in it with access you grant and can take away. When the engagement ends, nothing has to be handed over, because nothing was ever ours to hand.

This is the question most buyers forget to ask and most regret not asking. An agency that holds the code, the hosting or the domain holds the business, and the day you want to leave is the day you find out what that costs. Ask before the build, get the answer in the contract, and check that the accounts are in your name on the first day, not the last.

|  | Shopify store | Custom build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Right for | Physical products, fixed prices, a cart | A catalogue or a process the platform cannot model |
| Checkout | The platform's: well tested, hard to break | Yours to design, and yours to keep working |
| Speed | Fast until the apps pile up; audit quarterly | Fast until nobody owns it; name the owner |
| Cost | A theme and a set-up, priced on the call | Priced to the number, as software, after scoping |
| Who keeps it | You: the store, the theme, the domain | You: the repository, the hosting, the domain |
| Time to launch | Weeks | Months, and the scope decides how many |

### What does it cost, and what is not included?

Website development is not part of the Standard package; the pricing page says so in the exclusions rather than in small print. A Shopify set-up, the theme, the structure and the product presentation, is a smaller project than a custom build and is priced on the first call once we have seen what you sell. A custom build is Tailored, which means priced to the number it has to produce, after we have scoped it as software and not as a website with ambitions.

What a build does not include, whichever kind: the product photography, which no site survives without, and the ads that send people to it. Both are separate decisions, and both usually matter more to the result than the platform does.

### When do we say no?

When a custom build is wanted for reasons that are about the brand's self-image rather than the buyer's path to the checkout. When the budget for the site would leave nothing for the photography or the ads. When the site is to be built on a platform nobody on your side can operate after we leave. And when the real problem is the offer, which a new site will present more beautifully and not fix.

The right site is the one that gets out of the way between the ad and the order. Most of the time that is a Shopify store with a good theme and a ruthless edit. Some of the time it is software with a shop at the end of it. Tell us what you sell and the number you need from it, and we will tell you which.

## Getting your brand cited by AI search

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/how-to-get-your-brand-cited-by-ai-search/ · How we work · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

What an answer engine reads, how to write a page it will quote, the summary file, entity consistency, why listicles stopped being cited, and what this site does itself.

A growing share of the people who used to search and click now ask an assistant and read the answer. Your brand is either in that answer or it is not, and if it is not, you will never see the search that excluded you. This is what we have learned about getting quoted, applied to our own site first.

**The short version.** Answer the question in the first forty words of the page, in plain sentences, with the brand named. Publish an agent-readable summary file. Describe yourself the same way everywhere. Mark up the page's facts so a machine does not have to guess, and never mark up a fact the page does not state. Stop writing roundups; write the page about your own thing.

### What does an answer engine actually read?

An assistant answering a question does not read your site the way a visitor does. It fetches a handful of pages it believes are relevant, looks for passages that answer the question on their own, and assembles a reply from the ones it trusts, naming where they came from. Trust comes from the passage stating a checkable fact, from the page being about the thing asked, and from the same facts appearing elsewhere on the web without contradiction.

That has consequences for how a page is written. A paragraph that only makes sense after reading the three above it cannot be quoted. A page that takes six hundred words to arrive at the point will have its point missed. A claim with no number, no date and no name is not a fact the machine can use, so it uses someone else's.

### How do you write an answer-first passage?

Put the answer at the top. The question in the heading, phrased the way a person would ask it, and the answer in the first sentences beneath it, complete in itself. If someone read only that passage, they would have what they came for. Then the detail, for the reader who wants it.

Name the entity in the passage. An engine assembling an answer needs to know who is speaking. A passage that says we charge a flat fee is less useful to it than one that says Drifted Marketing charges a flat monthly fee, published on its pricing page, with advertising spend separate. The second one can be lifted out and still be true.

- One question per heading, written the way it is typed.
- The answer in the first forty words under it, complete on its own.
- One claim per paragraph, so a paragraph can be quoted without dragging its neighbours.
- A number with its date and its owner, or no number.
- The brand's name in the passage, not implied from the page.

### Why plain sentences?

Because an engine summarises, and adjectives do not survive summary. A sentence that says the results were exceptional gives the machine nothing to carry. A sentence that says what the result was, for whom, and when, gives it a fact, and facts are what get quoted.

Plain also means no acronyms. An assistant reading a page about return on ad spend will find the brand that wrote those words, not the one that wrote the four letters. Spell out the thing the number measures. It makes the page longer and it makes it quotable, and it has the side effect of making the page readable to the person who has not hired an agency before, who is the person searching.

### What is the agent-readable summary file?

A plain text file, published at llms.txt on your own domain, that tells an assistant who you are, what you do, where you are, what it costs and which pages matter. It is the one document on the web where you decide exactly how a machine describes you. A fuller version, llms-full.txt, can carry the important pages themselves, so an assistant does not have to crawl for them.

Ours opens with one line that says what Drifted Marketing is and where, then the services, the published fees and the clients we can name; the full version carries every piece in the journal. Both are generated from the same content files that build the site, so they cannot say something a page does not. That matters more than it sounds: a summary file that drifts from the site is a contradiction, and contradictions lower an engine's confidence in both.

Keep it factual and keep the top of it short. Anything in it is quotable, which is the point and the risk.

### What is entity consistency, and why does it matter?

An answer engine builds one picture of your business from many sources: your site, your Google listing, your Instagram profile, the directories, the pages that mention you. If those sources agree, the picture is confident. If your site says you are an agency in Karachi, your Google listing says a consultancy, and a directory lists an address you left last year, the engine has three weak entities instead of one strong one, and quotes none of them.

The fix is dull and effective. Choose one sentence about who you are, one name, one place, one description of what you do, and use it without variation everywhere a machine might read it. Check the listings once a quarter. When something changes, change it everywhere in the same week. Our own entity line is written once and read into the summary file and the structured data from that one place, so the two cannot drift apart.

### Why did comparison listicles stop being cited?

For a while the way to be cited was to write the roundup: the ten best agencies in your city, with yourself placed third for modesty. Engines quoted those pages because they looked like answers. They have since learned what a reader learned earlier: a roundup written by one of the entries is not a source, it is an advertisement, and it knows nothing first-hand about the other nine.

Engines now prefer the primary page. If the question is what an agency charges, the page that gets quoted is the agency's own pricing page, with a figure on it. If the question is how a campaign worked, it is the case page from the company that ran it, with the number and the date. A listicle has no first-hand knowledge, so it has nothing an engine cannot get better from the source.

So stop writing roundups and write the page about your own thing: what you charge, what you did, what you will not do. Concede something. A page that never admits a case where it is the wrong choice does not get quoted on a comparison question, because it does not read like a comparison.

### What is schema, in plain terms?

Structured data is a block of labelled facts inside the page's code, invisible to the reader, that tells a machine what the page is without making it guess: this is an organisation, this is its founder, this is an article published on this date by this person, these are the questions on the page and their answers. Search engines have read it for years. Answer engines read it as readily as they read the copy.

The rule is that it must only say what the page already says. Markup is tempting precisely because nobody sees it, which is why it must be held to the same standard as the copy. A rating the page never shows, a client the page never names, a number that was not cleared for the page: each is a lie that a machine will quote with your name attached.

| What the engine wants | What most pages do | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A passage that answers the question alone | Build to the point over six paragraphs | Put the answer under the heading, complete, then the detail |
| A named entity making a checkable claim | Say we, and reach for adjectives | Name the brand, give the number, date it |
| One consistent description across the web | A different bio on every profile | One sentence, everywhere, checked quarterly |
| A primary source | A roundup with yourself in it | The page about your own price, work and limits |
| Markup that matches the page | Markup that flatters it | Facts the page states, and nothing more |

### What does this site do itself?

Every page opens with the answer. The longer journal pieces carry question-shaped headings and a boxed short version with the same label every time, so the extractable answer can be found by pattern. The fees are published and read into the pages that quote them from one file, so an article cannot quote a price the pricing page has changed. The clients we name are named by company, with the work and, where one has been cleared, the number and its date.

The summary file and its full version are generated from the same content as the pages. The structured data describes the organisation, the founder, each article and each set of questions, and a check runs over all of it before the site builds: any figure not on the cleared list fails the build, a client result printed without its date fails the build, and any claim to be the first or the only fails the build. We built the gate because we made the mistakes it catches, four separate times, before it existed.

What none of this can do is make a weak offer quotable. An engine cites the page with the fact, and if there is no fact, there is nothing to cite. It does not replace classic search, which still sends most of the visitors. And no one can promise you a citation, because the engine decides, and it changes its mind. What you can do is give it no reason to doubt you, which is most of the work.

## Short-form video when you have never filmed

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/short-form-video-for-a-brand-that-has-never-filmed/ · Creator growth · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

The object is the content, one idea per beat, captions for muted viewing, what a shoot day looks like, and what a month of eight videos comes to.

Most brands that have never filmed think the obstacle is a camera or a presenter. It is neither. The obstacle is not knowing what the video is about, and the answer is almost always sitting on the shelf behind you.

**The short version.** Film the thing, not a person talking about the thing. Each video says one idea, in one beat. Write the captions as if the sound is off, because it is. A shoot day captures a month of material if the list is written first. Eight videos a month is a sustainable rhythm, and it is the one our Standard package is built around.

### What is the video about?

The object is the content. The product, the room, the process, the thing in the case. A brand that sells towels films the towel being made, folded, used. A museum films the jacket. A café films the bread coming out. None of these need a presenter, a script or a studio. They need a phone, a window and a reason the object is interesting, which you already know, because you chose to sell it.

This is the lesson from the short films we make for Gettysburg Museum of History. The collection sits in glass cases on open display: uniforms, equipment, the belongings of the people who carried them. We film the piece, write one line, and cut it for a vertical screen. Who wore it, where, and why it sits behind this glass. A jacket with a name on it stops the scroll in a way that a person saying the museum is worth visiting never will.

Objects beat adjectives. Your product does not need to be a century old for that to be true. It needs a detail a viewer can look at, and a line that tells them what they are looking at.

### Why one idea per beat?

A short video is not a shorter long video. It is one idea, delivered in one movement. The beat is the unit: a cut, a line, a reveal. A video that tries to say three things says none of them, because the viewer has decided whether to stay before the second one arrives.

In practice this means the first frame shows the object, the first line says the one thing, and the rest of the video earns the line. The overcoat he wore at the Bulge. The towel after a hundred washes. The dish that sells out by nine. One claim, then the proof of it, then stop. The ending is where most videos go wrong, because the maker keeps going after the idea has landed. Cut on the idea.

- One object in frame, not the whole shop.
- One line, written before the shoot, that the shot has to prove.
- One movement: a reveal, a fold, a pour, a hand turning the piece over.
- One ending, which is the moment the line is proven, and not a second later.

### Why write captions for muted viewing?

Because the sound is off. People watch in queues, in bed, at work, on trains, and the default on most phones is silence. A video that depends on its audio is a video most viewers never understood. The caption is not an accessibility afterthought. It is the script.

So the one line goes on screen, in words, in the first second. Large, in the brand's own type, placed where the platform's interface will not cover it. If there is speech, it is captioned in full, and the captions are checked by a person, because the automatic ones get names and products wrong. If there is music, it is a bonus for the minority who have the sound on, and nothing depends on it.

A useful test before posting: watch the video on mute with the brightness low. If you could not say what it was about, nobody scrolling past will.

### What happens on a shoot day?

A shoot day is a list, executed. Before anyone picks up a phone, there is a written shot list: the objects, the one line for each, the movement, the angle, the light. On the day, we work through the list in order, shooting more than we need of each so there is a choice in the edit. A well-planned day in one location produces a month of material. An unplanned day produces an afternoon of people wandering around with a camera.

What to have ready: the objects, clean and reachable; a window or a doorway for natural light; a table or a plain surface; the people who know the stories, for the lines we have not written yet. What not to do: tidy the place into something it is not. The workshop looks like a workshop. That is the content.

A shoot day on your premises is priced on its own, because the Standard package does not include on-site photography and videography; the pricing page says so in the exclusions rather than in a footnote. For a brand far from Karachi, the usual answer is that you film to our shot list on a phone, over a morning, and send us the footage. We write the list, we direct by message, we cut. The results are good because the list was good, not because the camera was.

### What does a month of eight videos look like?

Eight short videos a month is the rhythm the Standard package is built around, alongside six carousels, four posters and the rest of the loop, at $4,000 a month. Eight is two a week, which is enough for the platform to keep showing you to new people and few enough that each one gets made properly. A brand posting daily with nothing to say trains its audience to skip it.

| Week | The two videos | What they are for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One | The object, plainly; the object in use | Introduce the thing to people who have never seen it |
| Two | The process; the detail | Prove the claim: how it is made, what it is made of |
| Three | The question; the comparison | Start conversations and saves from people who are deciding |
| Four | The story; the month's best, recut | Give the people who stayed a reason to come back |

The recut in week four is deliberate. The video that performed best gets a new opening and goes out again. Most brands post a winner once and move on; the platform will happily show a good video to a new audience a second time if you let it.

What we report each month is what the videos did: reach, saves, how many people stayed past the opening, how many stayed to the end, and, where a video asked for something, whether people did it. Views alone are not in the report, because views do not pay invoices.

### What will we not do?

We will not fake customer-made video. A paid actor pretending to have discovered your product in their kitchen is a lie the platform's audience has learned to spot, and it costs the brand more trust than it earns in clicks. If you want real customers on camera, we ask real customers, and some say no.

We will not chase a trend because it is a trend. A format that is everywhere this week is a format the audience is tired of by the time your version is edited. We use a format when it serves the object and not otherwise.

And we will not promise reach. The platform decides who sees a video, and nobody who sells short-form video can honestly tell you in advance how far one will travel. What we can promise is the method: the object, one idea, captions, a list, eight a month, and a report that says what happened. The first video will be the worst one. The eighth will be better. That is how it goes for everyone, including brands that film.

## Meta ads: the first thirty days

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/meta-ads-the-first-thirty-days/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

What we do in each of the first four weeks of a Meta ads engagement, why we start with ten creatives, and what the numbers can and cannot tell you by week four.

A new ads engagement is judged on its first month, which is fair, as long as both sides agree in advance what a month can prove. This is what the first thirty days look like with us: week by week, what we do, what you see, and what we refuse to promise.

**The short version.** Week one is the call, the access and the number. Week two is the page and ten creatives. Week three, the ads go live on a small budget. Week four, you get the first honest report. Losers are cut every week from then on. The spend stays in your own ad account throughout, and the fee is flat.

### Week one: what happens on the call?

The first call is thirty minutes and there is no deck. We ask for the number you need, the margin on what you sell, and what a sale actually is for you: a checkout, a booking, a message, a cash-on-delivery order that may be refused at the door. Then we ask to look at the ad account, if there is one, before we say anything about what we think we can do.

The rest of week one is access and tracking. Your ad account, in your business manager, with us added as a user you can remove. The pixel and the conversion events checked against real orders, because an account optimising toward an event that fires twice per purchase is optimising toward fiction. If there is no account, we set one up in your name, on your card, and hand you the keys the same day.

We also agree, in writing, what the first report will measure. Cost per result against the number from the call. Not reach, not clicks, not video views, unless one of those is the result.

### Week two: why ten creatives?

Because we do not know which one will work, and neither does anyone else. An agency that launches with one hero ad is betting your first month on a guess. Ten creatives, each saying one thing in one format, let the platform and the audience tell us which argument lands. Some are a product on a plain background with one line. Some are a short video. Some are a question. The point is range, not polish.

- The product, plainly, with the price.
- The product in use, filmed on a phone, with captions for muted viewing.
- The objection, answered: what it costs to ship, how long it takes, what happens if it is wrong.
- The question that starts a conversation, for a brand that sells by message.
- The comparison, when the buyer is choosing between two things that look alike.

The second job of week two is the page. The ad is a promise and the page has to keep it, on a phone, in a few seconds. If the sale closes in a conversation, as it does for a brand that sells personalised products, the page is the inbox, and the creative is built to start a message rather than a click. Either way, nothing goes live until the place the ad sends people has been looked at by someone who is not us.

### Week three: what goes live, and how much do you spend?

The ads go live in week three, on a small budget. Small means enough to produce results we can read, not enough to hurt if the first week is wrong. We would rather spend a modest amount learning which three creatives deserve the budget than spend the whole month proving that seven of them did not.

The structure is simple on purpose: a handful of ad sets, broad audiences where the platform is good at finding buyers on its own, a retargeting set for people who have already met the brand, and the same ten creatives running against each. We check the account every morning your time. We do not touch it every morning, because the platform needs a few days of stable settings to learn, and an account that is adjusted daily never gets to.

What you see in week three is the ads themselves, in your own account, and a short note on what is running and why. What you do not see yet is a verdict. Three days of data is not a verdict, and anyone who gives you one is reading noise.

### Week four: what do the first numbers say?

By the end of week four there is a real report. It says what was spent, what came back, which creatives earned their budget and which were cut, and the cost per result against the number we agreed in week one. It is written in sentences, and the numbers in it come from your account, which you can open and check.

What it cannot say is whether the engagement works. A month is enough to find the first creatives that sell and the first that do not. It is not enough to know what the account does in a holiday week, or whether the cost of attention rises when more advertisers arrive, or how a second batch of creatives performs against the first. We say that on the call, and we say it again in the report, so that a good first month is not mistaken for a finished one.

### Why are losers cut every week?

From week four on, the account runs on a weekly rhythm. The creatives that cost more per result than the number we agreed are paused. The ones that beat it get more budget and get rebuilt: the same argument, a new opening, a new format. New creatives enter on a schedule, because every winning ad eventually tires, and the account needs its replacement ready before that happens rather than after.

This is the part of ads management that is unglamorous and that matters most. The launch is one week. The weekly cut is every week for as long as you are a client. Ask any agency how often it pauses an ad and what rule it uses to decide. The answer should be a threshold and a day of the week.

| Week | What we do | What you see |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One | The call, the number, the access, the tracking | A written note on what the first report will measure |
| Two | Ten creatives, and the page or the inbox | The creatives, for approval, in your voice |
| Three | Live on a small budget, broad plus retargeting | The ads running in your own account |
| Four | The first report; the first weekly cut | Spend, return, cost per result, what was paused and why |

### What did this produce for The Gallery?

The Gallery sells personalised newborn wear in Pakistan. Every order needs a conversation: a name, a spelling, a date, sometimes a photograph of the nursery. The checkout was already the direct message, so the campaign was built to start conversations rather than to send people to a product page, and it was optimised toward the inbox.

Ten creatives, cut weekly. The result, counted where the sale actually closed, was $5.20–$6 back per $1 of ad spend, every campaign to July 2026. Not an average across one good quarter: every campaign. The spend behind that return is not published, and we will not quote a return for your account before we have seen it. Nobody who guarantees a number is telling you the truth.

### Why does the spend stay in your own account?

Because the account is where the value accumulates. The pixel data, the audiences, the creative history and the results all live in it, and whoever owns the account owns them. If the agency runs your ads from its account, leaving means starting from nothing. If you own it, leaving means removing one user.

It also keeps the money honest. Your card pays the platform directly. Our fee is flat and separate, and we never take a percentage of what you spend, because an agency paid on spend is paid to spend. The cost to you is that you hold the keys: you approve the budget, and you will see every dollar leave. We think that is how it should feel.

The Starter package, at $2,000 a month, is Meta ads on one account with four new creatives a month, optimised weekly, with a monthly written report and a monthly call. Larger budgets and more than one platform are priced to the number. Either way, the thirty days above are the same thirty days, and the report at the end of them is the one you judge us on.

## Email marketing: the three emails that pay

https://driftedmarketing.com/blog/email-marketing-the-three-emails-that-pay/ · Performance media · by Umer Tariq · published 2026-10-22

A welcome, an abandoned checkout and a monthly note do most of the work email can do, and the open rate is not how you will know.

Email is the channel brands neglect because it is unglamorous and then rediscover because it is the only one they own. Nobody can change the algorithm on your list. The problem is that most lists are either silent or shouted at. Three emails fix most of that, and they are not complicated.

**The short version.** Set up a welcome email, an abandoned-checkout email and a monthly note. The first two run themselves once they are written; the third is the one you have to keep writing. Clean the list every quarter. Judge all of it on clicks and orders, never on opens, because opens are no longer a measure of anything.

### Why only three?

Because three is what a brand with one person on marketing will actually keep running. A twelve-email welcome sequence and a win-back flow with branching logic look impressive in a proposal and are abandoned by the second month, half-written, sending a broken link to everyone who signs up. Three emails, each with one job, can be written well, measured honestly and improved one at a time.

They also map to the three moments email is good at: someone has just arrived, someone was about to buy and did not, and the long quiet in between. Nearly everything else email is asked to do is one of those three in a costume.

### What should the welcome email say?

It goes the moment someone subscribes, and it has one job: to confirm that the person made a good decision. Not a discount, unless a discount was the reason they signed up, in which case it must be in the first line and work the first time. Who you are, in two sentences. The one product or piece to start with. A reply address that a human reads.

The welcome email is the best-opened message you will ever send, because the person just asked for it. That makes it the place to ask the question that shapes everything after: what are you here for. A single link per answer, and the answer tells you what to send next. Most brands waste this message on a logo and a coupon.

Write it once, properly, then leave it alone for a quarter. The temptation is to keep tinkering. The useful version of tinkering is reading the replies.

### What does the abandoned-checkout email do?

Someone put a product in the cart, reached the checkout, and left. The reasons are mundane: the shipping cost appeared, the phone rang, the card was in the other room. The abandoned-checkout email is a reminder, sent within the hour, that the thing is still there.

It should show the product, with its picture, and one button back to the checkout. It should not open with a discount. A brand that discounts every abandoned cart teaches its customers to abandon carts, and within a few months a share of your checkout traffic is people waiting for the email. If the first reminder does not work, a second a day later can answer the usual objection: here is what shipping costs, here is the returns policy, here is the one question people ask.

This is the email with the clearest return of any you will send, because it goes only to people who were already buying. It is also the one most stores have switched on with the platform's default copy, which reads like a receipt. Rewrite it in your own voice. It takes an hour.

### What goes in the monthly?

One story, one product, one ask. The monthly is the email that keeps the list warm between purchases, and its job is to be worth opening rather than to sell on the day.
